bio.en: Jeff Weinstein spent six-plus years at Stripe, where he led payment-infrastructure product teams, scaled Stripe Payments to hundreds of billions in annual volume, and grew Stripe Atlas—now used to start one in six new Delaware corporations.
bio.zh: Jeff Weinstein 在 Stripe 任职六年多，领导支付基础设施产品团队，将 Stripe Payments 的规模做到每年数千亿交易量，并壮大了 Stripe Atlas——如今全美每六家新成立的特拉华州公司就有一家通过它注册。

summary.en: Jeff breaks down the skills behind his remarkably effective product leadership: a go-go optimism and long-term compounding philosophy, operationalizing product craft and quality, and treating every customer complaint as an 'unbelievable gift' of direct signal. He shares the 'Stripe Study Groups' empathy practice he started (role-play as a customer with no agenda to solve problems), how to talk to customers, how to know you have product-market fit, and how to pick great metrics. The episode is the longest in Lenny's history for good reason—a full archaeology of a beloved product leader's craft.
summary.zh: Jeff 拆解了他极高效率的产品领导力背后的技能：积极进取的乐观主义与长期复利式的理念、把产品工艺与质量落到日常，以及把每条客户抱怨都当作直连信号的“不可思议的礼物”。他分享了发起的“Stripe 学习小组”共情练习（角色扮演成客户、不以解决问题为目的）、如何与客户交谈、如何判断你已找到产品市场契合，以及如何挑选好指标。这期节目成为 Lenny 史上最长的一期并非没有原因——它是对一位备受喜爱的产品领导者“手艺”的完整考古。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: The moment the customer felt compelled enough to go out of their way to talk about some problem, that's a unbelievable gift. I will leave a meeting to just get one message back to them. turns.zh: 当客户主动发声、愿意不遗余力地反馈问题时，这无疑是难得的馈赠。我曾为了一条回复而中断会议。若能与五到十位客户保持顺畅的短信沟通，你就能获得大量直接反馈，这些信息的感染力极强。

turns.en: Well, what was the value that we're trying to produce for the customer and can we measure it from their perspective? And okay, how do you know you have product market fit? Charts that showcase things are going up into the right on one hand and then tweets on the other.
turns.zh: 首先，我们要明确为客户创造的价值，并从他们的视角去衡量。如何判断产品与市场是否契合？关键在于观察数据曲线——一方面是业务量稳步增长，另一方面是客户反馈的推文。

turns.en: We show up four to eight people total pretend to be some company with some outcome problem. Rule one is you do not work at Stripe and rule two is we're not here to solve any problems. This is just about practicing empathy for the customer.

turns.speaker: Lenny

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I wanted to start with a quote that I found from you that I think gives a little perspective into how you think and how you approach the world. So here's the quote. turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Some of it was just the fact that I wasn't particularly good at the class and had to rationalize it for myself in some form. So in retrospect that sounds highfalutin, but at the time I just wasn't particularly good at the classes I was in. But I think it comes from growing up. I went to a pretty hippy-dippy K through 12 school in Baltimore, Maryland where we were really asked to think about why we were in school and to pick any of the courses that were of interest to us outside of AP programs or grades or any particular requirements. You really got to choose your own path. And I recall one particular class in high school, which was somewhat a science class, but it was called the History of Science, and we actually walked through and studied all of the, at the time, best understood ways the world worked in science, but then later were turned out to be wrong, right? (00:04:40): In the 1500s we believed X, Y, and Z. In the 1600s we believed A, B and C. just very confidently. In 1500s we thought something and then the 1600s we thought something very different. And so this class was quite impactful on me where we spent an entire year studying things that are not true. It was fascinating. That particular teacher employed another trick on us during that class, which was it took the tuition fee of our school and divided it by the number of hours and wrote the cost on a ticket and then handed us in the beginning of the year. Tickets for every single one of the classes and he would stand at the door and you would have to give him a ticket at the end of the class that he thought it was worth it. And just like that practice of deep intellectual understanding of how people evaluated something at the time and choosing for yourself to spend the time on it by just the physical act of handing that ticket to the teacher. (00:05:44): That really clicked for me. And so when I got to college and it was a real college university, people are coming from often quite more rigorous backgrounds of things that were true. I was a bit unprepared and I remember actually taking a microeconomics class that was quite advanced and had a close friend and we studied exactly the same information. We sat and looked at the same cheat sheets, we practiced the same quizzes, we read the same books, and he got the top grade in the class and I got the bottom and that's from where that quote came from where the professor said, I think you should bump, potentially bump down. I was like, "I already know that stuff. I'm interested in this topic. I'm going to try to improve, but look just because I'm significantly worse than the other kids in the class that has little to do with if I should leave." And he was particularly cool with it.

部分原因在于我当时对课程并不是很擅长，需要以某种方式为自己找借口。回想起来，这听起来挺冠冕堂皇的，但当时我确实不擅长所学的课程。不过我认为这源于成长经历。我在马里兰州巴尔的摩上了一所相当自由派的K-12学校，那里真的鼓励我们思考为什么要上学，并让我们自由选择除AP课程、成绩要求或特定要求之外的感兴趣课程。你真的可以自主规划自己的道路。我记得高中有一门课，表面上是科学课，但实际上叫做《科学史》。我们系统学习了当时人们对世界运作方式最深刻的理解，但后来这些观点被证明是错误的。比如16世纪人们认为X、Y、Z是正确的，17世纪又坚信A、B、C是正确的。人们曾对某些观点深信不疑，而后又推翻了原有认知。这门课对我影响很大，我们花了一整年时间研究那些后来被证明错误的理论，真是令人着迷。老师还有个绝招，他把学校的学费总额除以课时数，写在票券上，年初发给每个学生。每节课结束后，学生都要把票券交给老师，证明这节课值得花时间。这次经历让我深刻体会到，人们如何评估当时的知识体系，以及如何通过亲手将票券交给老师这种行为来选择是否投入精力钻研。

到了大学，面对真正严苛的学术要求时，我明显准备不足。记得我选了一门微观经济学高级课程，同桌学霸和我是同步学习的。我们用完全相同的笔记、刷相同的题库、读相同的教材，但他拿了班上第一，我却垫底。这就是教授说"你或许该降低期望"的由来。我反驳道："这些知识我都懂，我对这课感兴趣。我会努力提升，但成绩差跟退学没关系。"教授倒很理解。
