turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: It did take a change though because I started in... English was my selected major in school, but then I kept playing with computers and I kept liking math and I looked at the roles of the backgrounds of the people who were running the types of companies I loved. At the time Facebook was getting super phenomenally successful. Apple was already on their up and up again and everyone who was leading those places had technical backgrounds and I liked computers a lot, so I added computer science as an engineering degree midway through school. So I had to take the real science classes with the pre-med kids and the rest of it, and I did similarly poorly, but I did end up with a computer science degree and a liberal arts degree. So it was a journey, but I had to make a pretty big switch in the middle to get on that path.
turns.zh: 确实需要做出改变，因为我最初选的专业是英语，但后来我一直沉迷于电脑，热爱数学，还留意那些运营我喜爱的公司的管理者的背景。当时，Facebook正红极一时。苹果也已重振旗鼓，而那些行业领军人物都拥有技术背景。由于我对计算机的浓厚兴趣，中途我转修了计算机科学学位。这意味着我必须与医学预科生一起上真正的科学课程，成绩同样不理想，但最终我获得了计算机科学和文科双学位。整个过程充满挑战，但为了踏上成功之路，我不得不做出重大转变。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I asked you if there was one thing that you'd love to get across in this podcast. I asked you what would it be and here's what you said. Here's the first item on this list that you sent me, "Go, go, go ASAP plus optimistic comma, long-term compounding approach." Can you just talk about what you mean by that?
turns.zh: 我之前问过你，是否有想在本期播客中传达的核心理念。你当时给出的回答是：“立即行动，保持乐观，坚持长期复利策略。” 能否请你详细解释一下这句话的含义？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Yeah, there's two things going on here. So I see the world as immediately we have just such opportunity to take action in front of us. We can be optimistic and go, go, go as soon as possible. I think that a lot of life is you get as much furniture as you've room in the house. We will do the work the night before it's due, so let's just make it due tomorrow. Can we turn tomorrow into today? So just optimistically seeing if we can just inject energy to go, go, go has produced surprising results and I think it ignites in other people that same interest and then it feeds off each other. And that's I think really in my bones from growing up. And then I added over time, had to learn this longer term, compounding, more strategic mindset where some of the things we want to accomplish, be it at my startups in the past or at Stripe, they can't be solved in an afternoon. (00:11:41): They're going to require layers of infrastructure and services and applications and UI and partnerships that really look like that iceberg drawing you see where you just see the top, but then there's the whole thing underneath and I've had to learn over time to pair my instinct of like, "Let's get it done today, let's move forward, let's see what we can get done. Let's make some mistakes, let's try it out." With, "Where are we going? What needs to be true over time? Where can we always invest? What will we never regret spending time in?" We'll never regret spending time making the latency of our payments APIs at Stripe faster. We'll never regret making it more reliable to send 83B election mails to the IRS. Like we'll never regret those things. So let's just always compound those capabilities over time. Then the trick is how do you mix this go, go, go attitude with a long-term compounding? That's something I still struggle with, but I try to purposely balance it more than I used to.
turns.zh: 这句话背后有两个层面的含义。首先，我认为人生充满即时机遇。我们应该保持乐观，尽快行动。正如俗话所说：“人生就像打包行李——你能装多少就装多少。” 我们常把任务拖到截止日期前才开始完成，但能否把明天变为今天呢？这种乐观的行动力能激发他人的兴趣，并形成良性循环。这是我的成长经历所深信的。随着时间推移，我逐渐领悟到，长期复利策略更为重要。比如，我在创业公司或Stripe面临的挑战，不可能在一天内解决。这需要层层搭建基础设施、服务、应用、用户界面和合作伙伴关系，就像冰山理论——我们只能看到冰山一角，但深层结构更为复杂。我必须平衡“今天就做”、“勇往直前”、“敢于犯错”的冲动，与“长期规划”、“持续投入”、“不留遗憾”的理性。比如，我们毫不犹豫地优化Stripe支付API的延迟，毫不犹豫地确保向IRS发送83亿份选举邮件的可靠性。这些决策都值得回味。因此，关键在于如何将即时行动力与长期复利策略相结合。这仍是我需要不断修炼的平衡之道。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's such a good way of summarizing just how to be successful in a lot of things. Go, go, go ASAP, stay optimistic. Focus on long-term compounding growth. Is there an example of that in action? I know we're going to talk about Atlas a bunch, but I guess is there an example of that working for you or a product you worked on?
turns.zh: 这真是总结成功秘诀的绝佳方式：立即行动，保持乐观，专注长期复利。能否举个实际案例？虽然我们会重点探讨Atlas，但你是否有其他成功案例或产品经历可以分享？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I work at Stripe, which is a infrastructure company. We build things that help businesses do online commerce in various forms, and I've had a few roles at Stripe. I'm in our beautiful office here in South San Francisco, one of which was the product person that helped us decide how we were going to go global and how we were going to offer multiple ways for people to pay. It turns out there's more than just credit cards in the world. There's small hundreds of ways that people will naturally want to pay for things online and as a business you're going to, of course, just want to accept whatever it is people want to pay with. And for the first seven or eight years of Stripe, well prior to my being here, the incremental country ads and the incremental new payment methods was relatively flat over time and that was surprising to all of us who worked here because the world wanted it and we had a lot of people working on it and we were working very hard, but it wasn't producing returns in the way that we wanted. (00:14:11): And so actually the optimistic as soon as possible go-go attitude was not working. No matter how much energy we poured into building Thailand payment methods or UK bank transfers or an in-person payment system in Latin America, we just couldn't rack up points and get it done. So we had to step back and say, "Well, what is the world going to look like in 10 years? What was going to need to be true and how can we start to go there now?" Which meant going a lot slower, building internal platforms, sending people around the world to start to build these payment methods, uproot their lives, pay for their apartments, get them on airplanes, start using these payment methods actually in the world. And so it really our line flat line for a while and we're like, "Okay, is this strategy working? Is it not working?" But then over time we start to see it switch to nonlinear again and go from whatever it was, 10 payment methods at the time. (00:15:03): And now Stripe accepts over 100. So we got to 50 really quickly and then skyrocketed to 100. And I remember there being a meeting where we said, "Well, maybe we should just lock everyone in the basement and see if we can get from 10 to 50." That would be the intensity startup go attitude. But we looked at the individual components of what it meant to get this done and how long we wanted this to be true for and we had to go a lot slower. That was a very formative decision where you had to mix the go, go, go with the long-term compounding.
turns.zh:
我在Stripe工作，这是一家基础设施公司。我们开发的工具帮助企业以各种形式开展在线商务。我在Stripe担任过多个职位，目前在南旧金山的漂亮办公室工作。其中一项工作是产品经理，负责指导我们如何实现全球化扩张，以及如何提供多样化的支付方式。事实上，世界上存在着数百种人们自然倾向于在线支付的方式。作为企业，您当然希望接受用户愿意使用的任何支付方式。在Stripe成立的前七八年，即我在加入之前，全球扩张和新增支付方式的进展一直停滞不前。这让我们所有员工都感到惊讶——毕竟全球市场需求巨大，我们投入了大量人力却未能如期达成目标。

（00:14:11）最初那种急于求成的冲动并不奏效。无论我们投入多少精力开发泰国支付方式、英国银行转账服务，还是拉丁美洲的线下支付系统，都未能取得成效。于是我们不得不退一步思考："十年后世界会是什么样子？我们需要达成哪些目标，又该如何从现在开始着手？"这意味着要放慢节奏，搭建内部平台，派遣员工前往全球各地开发支付方式，改变他们的生活方式，支付他们的房租，让他们登上飞机，在现实世界中真正使用这些支付方式。最初进展停滞不前，我们开始怀疑"这项策略是否有效？"但随着时间推移，情况再次出现非线性增长。从当时的10种支付方式，到现在Stripe支持的100多种支付方式。我们迅速突破50种，随后直线攀升至100种。我记得当时开会时有人提议："不如把所有人关在地下室里，看看能否从10种快速提升到50种。" 这正是典型的初创公司急于求成的态度。但我们仔细分析了实现这一目标的各个组成部分，以及期望实现的时间框架，最终不得不放慢节奏。这是一个至关重要的决策，既要保持进取心，又要兼顾长期复利效应。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. Okay, so let's start to delve deeper into some of the specific seals that I hear you're incredible at and that I've seen you be incredible at on Twitter and LinkedIn and things like that. So the first is craft, craft and quality. I'm told by many people that you have a very strong obsession with craft and user experience and quality and even more so I'm told that you teach people at Stripe how to be obsessed with craft and quality and user experience in a very systematic way. I feel like this is something a lot of people are starting to realize is really important and or are trying to get better at, either personally or at their company. So first of all, let me just ask why is this so important to you? Why do you think craft and experience and quality is so important? Why do you put so much emphasis on it yourself?
turns.zh: 太棒了。好的，接下来我们深入探讨一些你特别擅长的领域。我在推特和领英上看到很多人说你在这方面非常出色。我想了解一下具体的秘诀。首先是工艺、质量和用户体验。很多人告诉我，你对工艺、用户体验和质量有着极高的执着度，而且据说你还以非常系统化的方式教导Stripe的员工如何关注这些方面。我觉得这正是许多人开始意识到的重要性，或者正努力在个人或公司层面提升这方面的能力。所以首先，我想问你为什么对这些如此重视？你为什么认为工艺、体验和质量如此重要？你自己又为何如此强调它们？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I think I'm really working backwards from failures in the past and avoiding them. And so maybe just a quick story. I started a company several years ago based on just a personal pet peeve of mine, which was I was a SQL analyst. Many you listening might have written SQL in the past, maybe the robots write the SQL for you now, but you still need to write SQL yourself. And every single time I wrote a SQL query, I wanted to run the same subsequent analysis. I wanted great version control, I wanted all the cool stuff that GitHub had for code but for writing data code. And so my friends and I built a little Python tool which basically let you run our style queries. It lets you draw charts and pivot tables quickly and sharing all this modern SaaS application stuff. But applied to SQL a few years ago and we turned that into a company. (00:17:29): We got some progress, but then there was this moment one day where we had maybe a couple 100 customers and we had an error where we basically by accidentally shut down the service and it was bricked for 10 or 20 minutes. And at the time we were hustling in our little dinky office to get the application back online. And we really were proud of ourselves about how reasonably quickly we did and people went back to using it. It wasn't a super long outage and we didn't lose any data. We were just high-fiving each other. And we went about our day and about a year later I realized that that was a... (00:18:11): I missed a huge moment that I should have pounced on, which is that during those 20 minutes, our customers weren't furious. They weren't emailing us like crazy, they weren't texting us, they weren't trying to find us on Google Maps and knock on our door and say, "Hey, I need this thing back online immediately." We heard a couple comments from them, it was little murmurs. And I didn't realize at the time that was the signal that we did not have product market fit. And I ended up wasting many more years on that project. And wasting is a big word. We built amazing software, people liked it, we were able to sell the company. (00:18:55): It helped many of us learn how to really build software. But I'm really trying to avoid that situation again. And I think craft is a dessert that you get after the meal of does your thing solve a real problem in the world and are people clamoring, needing it badly? And that's really my obsession is in finding problems in which people will pause their entire day to solve. They will leap through the computer to be like, "Oh my God, I have that problem. Do you have a solution?" (00:19:32): And if you focus on that style of product development and we can get into just how do you listen for that and then turn that into product. Later, you might get the opportunity to really provide craft and beauty and touches and moments and delight. But certainly there is no amount of craft, there is no amount of beauty, there's no amount delight or touches you can add to a thing that will solve the problem we had at our startup, which is that people didn't really need this. And that's the biggest error is picking something in which people don't really need it. And then going through these practices of trying to make it great when maybe it shouldn't exist in the first place.
turns.zh:
我觉得自己现在做事的方法，就是从过去的失败中不断总结经验，努力避免重蹈覆辙。或许我可以讲个小故事。几年前，我创办了一家公司，起因是自己对 SQL 分析师工作的深恶痛疾。相信在座很多听众都曾写过 SQL 代码，或许现在由机器代劳，但终究还是要亲自编写查询语句。每次写 SQL 查询时，我都想顺便运行后续分析。我渴望完善的版本控制，渴望像 GitHub 一样为数据编写代码提供的所有酷炫功能。于是我和朋友们开发了一个 Python 工具，基本能实现自定义查询风格，还能快速生成图表和数据透视表，并支持所有现代 SaaS 应用的共享功能。但几年前将其应用于 SQL 领域后，我们把它发展成了一家公司。

（00:17:29）：我们取得了一些进展，但有一天出现了重大危机——当时我们有几百个客户，却因意外关闭服务器导致数据中断 10 到 20 分钟。当时我们在狭小的办公室里手忙脚乱地恢复服务，庆幸能迅速恢复运营，用户很快回归使用。停机时间不算太长，也没丢失数据，我们甚至互相击掌庆祝。然而一年后我意识到，那其实是……（00:18:11）：我错失了一个关键机会——在那 20 分钟里，用户并未暴跳如雷。他们没有狂发邮件、发短信，也没在谷歌地图上定位我们的办公室敲门求助。我们只听到几声抱怨，几乎没有抗议声。当时我没意识到，这是产品与市场不契合的信号。结果我又在那个项目上浪费了多年光阴。“浪费”这个词太严重了。我们开发了出色的软件，用户反响不错，最终成功出售公司。这段经历让我们学会了如何真正打造软件。但我现在决心避免重蹈覆辙。我认为“工艺”就像餐后甜点——当你的产品能解决真实世界的问题，用户迫切需求时，它才有意义。我的执着在于寻找那种让人们愿意暂停日常工作去解决的难题。他们会迫不及待地冲向电脑问：“天啊，我也遇到这种问题了，你有解决方案吗？”（00:19:32）如果你专注于这种产品开发理念，确实能学会如何捕捉用户需求并转化为产品。未来或许还有机会打造出精美绝伦的体验，但再多的精巧设计、美学追求或细节打磨，也无法解决我们初创公司遇到的根本问题——用户根本不需要这个产品。选择用户不需要的产品，再用各种技巧包装它，最终不过是徒劳。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think a lot of people see all these tweets and messages about just obsessed with the craft of what you're building and you can easily lose sight of... Nobody even cares about what you're building. It could be the most incredible experience ever designed, but if it's not something anyone ever wants, it doesn't really matter.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多人看到那些推特和消息时，只会沉浸在自己正在打造的项目中，却很容易忽视一个关键点……根本没人关心你做的这个东西。即便它是史上最惊艳的体验设计，但如果没人愿意使用，那也毫无意义。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: People don't really get out of bed for their second problem. They get out of bed for their first problem. And you have to carefully listen and not pitch your customer or your prospective customer as you're trying to figure this out. And I think this advice, not even advice just style applies to small companies, big companies, anyone which is people don't want to be pitched. I'm sometimes on a UXR call with a very well-meaning person or a founder who has a new product that they want advice on or they want to find customers. And the first thing that they start talking about when we get on the call is, "Hi, I'm the CEO of X, Y, and Z company. We do one, two, and three. I want to show you a demo." It's like, "Hold up, I'm a customer. I have..." What a wasted opportunity you've just done here. (00:21:34): I have so many problems, you're guessing ahead of time, what is my top problem and now that you've anchored and limited to the pitch you're going to miss, you very likely going to miss the burning problem that they have on the top of their mind. And it's not the customer's job to interrupt you and say, "Hey, could you stop your pitch? I want to tell you about my top problem." And you can see this down the stream, which then companies who launch things, put craft, have a great launch, raise money are then later gone. And it's because they built something that wasn't solving a burning need. And I think you can stem it all the way back to they were just pitching rather than sitting in silence and just waiting for their customer to just open their heart out about what's the most burning thing. (00:22:28): And sometimes I'll prompt our customers, I'll say, "Hey, do you mind just opening up your email? What's in there?" Or, "If you weren't talking to me right now, what would you be working on?" Or, "Hey, last week, what grinds your gears? What are you not looking forward to?" Or magic wand, "What do you wish you could just have off your plate immediately? Forget Stripe, forget about thing, work on just in your whole life. What is it that you do not want to be doing?" Or, "A massive opportunity you wish was just one door away?" And it's a little awkward because they don't know why you're asking that kind of question, but then you just sit there in silence. And for the most part, if you have amazing customers who are smart and ambitious and are trying to build their own business, they're going to want to offload their hardest thing to somebody else. (00:23:17): If you've earned trust along the way, and certainly not pitching is a great way of earning trust. You're just listening. We've learned a lot at Stripe from that. And that's where you can start to find adjacencies, right? "Well, hey, I don't know if Stripe could really help me with this, but wouldn't it be cool if we could identify if the person signing up on our site wasn't fraudulent or is who they say they are or isn't a bot, or are they really a dog on the internet?" And we're like, "We keep this as the major complaint from all of our customers, but we're not an identity company." It's like, "Well, I guess now we are because all of our customers who are trying to build their business all have this problem." And so via silence, you can just create your roadmap pretty quickly and drop a lot of the long UXR, long survey, long build cycle approach.
turns.zh: 人们通常不会因为第二个问题而起床。他们会因为第一个问题而起床。在试图解决问题时，你必须仔细倾听，避免向客户或潜在客户推销产品。我认为这种建议——甚至不算建议，只是一种处事风格——适用于小公司、大公司以及任何人。人们都不喜欢被推销。我有时会参加用户体验研究（UXR）电话会议，对方可能是怀着好意的创业者，或者是想寻求建议或寻找客户的新产品创始人。但电话一接通，他们首先开口就是：“我是X、Y、Z公司的CEO，我们做一、二、三件事。我想给您演示一下。”这时我会打断他们说：“等等，我是客户。我有……” 你刚刚浪费了一个绝佳的机会。（00:21:34）：我有太多问题，而你提前就猜测我的首要问题，这样一来你就局限了自己的思路，很可能错过客户最紧迫的需求。客户又不会主动打断你说：“嘿，别推销了，让我告诉你我的首要问题。”你可以从后续结果中看到，许多推出的产品虽然精心设计、宣传得很好、成功融资，但最终还是失败了。原因在于他们没有解决真正紧迫的需求。我认为这可以追溯到他们只是在推销产品，而不是耐心倾听客户的心声，等待客户主动敞开心扉，告诉你他们最迫切的需求。（00:22:28）：有时我会引导客户，比如问：“嘿，你介意打开邮箱看看吗？里面有什么？”或者：“如果你现在不和我通话，你会忙什么？” 或者：“上周什么事让你最烦躁？” 或者“最想立刻摆脱的烦心事是什么？忘掉Stripe，忘掉其他事，全心全意专注于你的事业吧。你最不想做什么？” 或者“一个近在咫尺的巨大机遇？” 这有点尴尬，因为他们不知道你为什么问这些问题，但你只需静静倾听。大多数情况下，如果客户聪明、有抱负、正在努力创业，他们会愿意把最棘手的问题交给别人解决。（00:23:17）：如果你赢得了信任（当然，推销产品绝非赢得信任的良方），你只需倾听。我们在Stripe从中收获颇丰。这就是你能开始寻找关联性的机会。比如：“嗯，我不知道Stripe能否帮我解决这个问题，但如果能识别出在我们网站注册的人是否是欺诈者、是否是真实身份、是否是机器人，或者他们是不是真的互联网上的‘狗肉号’，那不是很棒吗？”我们会说：“这原本是我们所有客户的主要抱怨，但我们不是身份验证公司。” 但客户会说：“好吧，看来现在我们就是了。因为所有想创业的客户都面临这个问题。” 这样通过倾听，你就能迅速制定路线图，省去冗长的用户体验研究、长篇问卷调查和漫长的开发周期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So I love where we're going with this. This is where I was going to actually talk about next is just your ability to talk to customers and user research. It feels very unique, watching you operate on Twitter, you're just sharing your email constantly, getting on calls with people constantly. There's this, you're breaking this wall between... That a lot of people imagine there is between the PM and the lead of a team and the customer. You're not relying easy research. You're not waiting for someone else to do this work for you. Talk about just why and how you do this. I think there's so much to learn from just how you operate in finding opportunities, picking problems to solve by talking to customers.
turns.zh: 嗯，我很赞同我们接下来的方向。接下来我要讲的是你与客户沟通和用户研究的能力。这真的很独特——看你如何在推特上运作，你不断分享邮箱，频繁与用户通话。你打破了很多人想象中产品经理、团队负责人和客户之间的那堵隔阂。你不依赖于被动的研究，也不等着别人来替你做这项工作。能否谈谈你为何要这样做，以及具体做法？我觉得从你寻找机会、通过与客户交流选定待解决问题的整个运作流程中，我们能学到很多东西。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: It's where the business comes from is customers. It is not a long shot hypothesis about why to talk to them. It's like if they love your stuff, they will tell their friends and pay fair prices for the product. We're so fortunate through the internet that people announced themselves as being interested in a topic. Sometimes they're interested in it by posting on Reddit a long thread or a screenshot of a customer service interaction that bugged them or hopeful that from their dorm room in country X, someone else in the world has solved the same problem. And the internet has given us all this absolutely magical forum that you can just yell out the window and then billions of people could actually listen to what you said out the window. Now, that's not all the time true for all people in all situations, but dramatically more true now than ever before in human history. (00:26:05): And so the fact that people wouldn't be listening to their customers and really jumping through the computer to talk to them surprises me. It's like I always sometimes think, "Do they have some other strategy? Are they so confident in what they're building that they don't need to hear directly from the people who will be using it?" And I think some of it is my own fear that I'm going to make the same mistake I've made in the past, which is build something that people like they're using but isn't solving a burning enough problem such that they're going to stop their day, they're going to tell their friends, we're going to be able to sustain the company economically over a long period of time. And that really just comes from hearing people's most burning problems and then just jumping through the computer and talking to them takes a little bit of nervous gumption, like walking up to a person at a bar or cocktail party and saying, "Hi, my name is Jeff." (00:27:08): It can be a little awkward, but then you get it. It's a rush once it starts to work. And once you get the iterative loop that they're excited to talk to you, they have problems, they see you as a trusted, not salesy, not pitching, not narrow-minded to just my product and my position, but I'm here to hear about all of your problems and see where we can help. Not promising we can help solve everything, but let's listen. That is infectious, both between the customers and internally. And so I'm able to bring more people into that practice. At Stripe, I'm able to quickly grab an engineer and hop on a call. I can forward a message over to a Slack group. And they know that because the customer's speaking directly, it somewhat trumps everything that's happening during the day. We could go to our meeting where we're going to guess what the customer wants or we could talk to them directly. (00:28:08): And you have to use a little bit of art to decide which customers you want to listen the closest to. But even at Stripe's scale, where we're dealing with many millions of businesses and many hundreds of millions of consumers on the other end of those businesses, you can pattern match relatively quickly. What are the styles of customers that represent where the world is going, the most ambitious, the most technical, the fastest growing, the most detailed. And you don't need 10,000 of those people to talk to. If you're text message friendly with five or 10 of those, you are going to have so much direct signal about where to go that you forget how you did it in the past.
turns.zh:
业务的根源在于客户。这并非凭空臆测为何要与客户沟通的理论。若他们真心喜爱你的产品，就会向朋友推荐，并为之支付合理价格。得益于互联网，人们能主动表达兴趣——有时他们会在Reddit上长篇发帖，分享困扰他们的客服互动截图，或怀着希望在异国他乡的宿舍里，期待全球某个角落有人解决了同样的问题。互联网为我们提供了神奇的交流平台，你只需在窗口呼喊，亿万人就能听到你的声音。当然，这并非适用于所有情况和所有人群，但当下比人类历史上任何时期都更普及得多。

（00:26:05）令人惊讶的是，竟有公司不愿倾听客户意见、主动跨越屏幕与他们对话。我有时会想：“他们是不是另有高招？他们对自家产品如此自信，以至于无需直接听取用户意见？”或许这源于我对自己过往错误的担忧——打造出人们喜欢使用但未能真正解决痛点的产品，导致他们无法停下手头事务、向朋友推荐，最终难以支撑公司的长期经济生存。关键在于倾听用户最迫切的需求，跨越屏幕与他们对话。这就像在酒吧或鸡尾酒会上主动搭讪：“你好，我叫杰夫。”（00:27:08）虽然略显尴尬，但一旦成功，回报惊人。当用户兴奋地与你交流问题时，他们会视你为值得信赖的伙伴——非推销型、非狭隘、非强加产品与立场，而是真诚倾听所有问题。这种正向循环在客户与内部团队间双向传递，因此我能将更多人引入这种实践。在Stripe，我能迅速召集工程师参与通话，将消息转发至Slack群组。客户直言不讳的反馈天然凌驾于日常会议的猜测之上——与其在会上猜测用户需求，不如直接倾听。（00:28:08）如何锁定最具洞察力的客户群体？即便在Stripe这样处理数百万商家、数亿消费者的平台上，相对快速的模式匹配也能奏效：识别代表行业发展方向、最具雄心、技术最强、增长最快、最具洞察力的客户群体。无需面面俱到，仅与5到10位客户保持短信沟通，你就能获得指引方向的直接信号，忘却过去的迷茫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love these. So I'd love to learn more about these tactics that you've found helpful. So you've shared this idea of silence, talking to someone and just being silent, and I forget the phrase you used, but just like ideas emerge, like your whole road map can emerge from that silence. So let me share a few of the things you shared so far and I'm curious what else. Two is tweeting just like, "Hey, I'm looking to improve Atlas right now. What bugs do you have? Here's my email address." You talked about text messaging, just like, "Hey, can I get your number? And I'll just text you when I have questions." If there's anything else to add to these, that'd be awesome. And then what else have you found? Just ways to actually get to a customer and find opportunities that are important.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这些了。所以我很想深入了解你发现的这些有效策略。你提到了保持沉默的技巧，就是在与人交谈时保持安静。我记不清你具体用的哪个词了，但正是通过这种沉默，灵感往往涌现，整个解决方案可能就此浮现。接下来让我分享一下你目前提到的几个点，我很想听听还有什么其他心得。第二点是发推文，比如“嘿，我现在正致力于改进Atlas产品。你们有什么问题吗？我的邮箱是……”。你还提到了发短信，比如“嘿，能留个电话号码吗？有问题我就发短信联系你”。如果还有其他补充，那就太棒了。那么你还发现了什么？具体有哪些方法能真正接触到客户，挖掘关键机遇呢？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Speed is an important one, which is just reducing the time between the moment the customer felt compelled enough to go out of their way to talk about some problem. They're busy, there are snacks to eat, they have families, they have other things to do. There's a lot going on in the world, a lot. Your dumb product, it's amazing that they would spend any of their time discussing it at all. I mean, most of the time if you don't like something, you just move along. You just apathetically, silently move forward in the world. And so the fact that someone took their finite time to succinctly with curiosity, communicate to the world or you about your product, that's a unbelievable gift. (00:30:27): That should be P-zero alert level intensity. And so I will leave a meeting, I will change what I'm doing to just get one message back to them. Even if it's, "Hey, I got this. I'm about to go to dinner. Can I hit you up tomorrow?" They're like, "Oh yeah, thank you. Awesome. I can't even believe you responded." That puts us in the camp of on the right trajectory where they're going to feel that they have a almost secret portal between this big brand of a company and another human who's just actually curious...
turns.zh: 速度至关重要，就是要缩短客户主动发声的时间。他们很忙，要吃零食、照顾家人、处理各种事务。世界上的事情太多了，太多了。你的产品再平庸，他们肯花时间讨论就已经很了不起了。大多数时候，如果不喜欢某个产品，直接就略过了。人们往往冷漠地、默默地生活着。所以有人愿意抽出宝贵的时间，带着好奇心向你传达对产品的看法，这简直是天大的恩赐。（00:30:27）这时候就得拉响P-0级警报了。我会立刻暂停手头的事，专心回复他们。哪怕只是回一句“好的，我现在要去吃晚饭了。明天再聊。”对方也会感激不尽：“天哪，太感谢你了。你回复得太快了！” 这样一来，客户就会觉得自己与大品牌之间建立了一种近乎神秘的沟通渠道——一个真心好奇、愿意倾听的人……

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: ... brand of a company and another human who's just actually curious what's going on, that's night and day. And it's also, fun fact, tip, when people are really hot on an issue and it could blow up on social or they're going to start becoming a detractor, we make mistakes, we have SLA breaches, we have errors, you're going to want to get on that stuff fast. And in those situations, my bar for how we will respond to those folks is not to just solve the problem, but it is to turn them into a promoter, and most of the time we're able to, even if there was a pretty relevant issue. (00:31:40): I remember one time at Atlas, we had this bug in which for a handful of our legal docs, they were handing out let's say, 25 shares rather than 25% of the shares. We dropped the percentage sign, and thankfully a founder noticed this in the docs and tweeted about it. My heart paused and I was like, "Oh no, this could be a really serious issue." And we were able to fix it and regenerate the documents relatively quickly for everyone that was impacted. And I was thinking to myself, "Wow, we really let this person down. We have one job to do, which is to get their company right and we didn't." (00:32:20): And that person was incredibly gracious about the situation and said, "Anytime you want me to just read your docs, I'd be happy to. I have a law degree. I care about this topic. I want to brainstorm with you about ways that Atlas could do more document creations." I was like, "Wow, I can't believe I was in this sort of defense position, and now we've gained a friend in the world who can be eyes and ears and brainstorm with us." And the team maintains a really close relationship with that person as they do with many, many founders who use Atlas. (00:32:53): And so, just again, we're so quick to put the outside world in this other camp where we need to touch it with kid gloves and treat it as a big blob and a cohort and a statistic, when it is a human with a problem who likes snacks, who is busy, and it's fun to do and it turns out to be an incredibly easy, fast way to figure out what to build.
turns.zh:
......一家公司的品牌，以及另一个真正好奇事情进展的人，这两者天壤之别。还有一个有趣的小贴士：当人们对某个问题反应激烈，可能会在社交媒体上引发风波，或者即将变成反对者时，我们必须迅速处理。即便问题涉及重大隐患，我们也要确保将他们转化为拥护者，而不是仅仅解决问题。这里有个关键点：我们要让用户不仅满意，还要让他们成为我们的忠实拥护者。

（00:31:40）：我记得在Atlas公司时，我们曾遇到一个漏洞——部分法律文件中的股份分配比例标注的是25股，而不是25%。我们把百分比符号去掉了，幸好有位创始人在文档中发现了这个问题并发推告知。我当时心一沉，心想：“天哪，这可能是个大问题。”最终我们迅速修复了问题，为受影响的用户重新生成了文件。我暗自思忖：“哇，我们真让这位用户失望了。我们的核心职责是帮助他们把公司做好，而这次却没做到。”

（00:32:20）：不过那位用户非常善解人意，主动说：“随时欢迎让我审阅你们的文档。我有法律学位，对这个领域很关注，愿意和你们一起探讨Atlas如何优化文档创作。”我感慨道：“真不敢相信我之前还处于防御状态，现在却收获了一位能为我们出谋献策的伙伴。”如今，团队与这位用户以及众多使用Atlas的创始人保持着密切合作。

（00:32:53）：所以，我们总习惯把外界看作需要谨慎应对的群体，仿佛他们是冰冷的数据、统计数字和群体。但实际上，他们也是有血有肉的人——他们喜欢零食，忙碌于日常，乐于参与互动。事实证明，迅速识别并解决问题是构建成功产品的捷径。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a bunch of stuff I want to follow up here. One is, people may be hearing this and like, "Oh my God, I'd be overwhelmed with feedback and people to fix problems for and bugs and texting of people." They're just like, "There's so many people that potentially I'd have to be interacting with." How do you try to narrow that down? I know Atlas is a very highly adopted product. There's a ton of people, there's probably bugs, often people sending you feedback. How do you pick the people to zero in on?
turns.zh: 这里有几个问题我想进一步探讨。首先，听众可能会想：“天哪，面对如此多的反馈、问题、漏洞和用户需求，我肯定会应接不暇。”他们会担心需要同时与大量用户沟通。你们是如何筛选重点的？据我所知，Atlas是一款应用广泛的产品，用户众多，难免会遇到漏洞，用户也会频繁反馈。你们如何锁定关键用户？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I think there are two parts to this. One, what a problem to have. Of all the problems in the world, "I'm overwhelmed by customer interest," is on the top list of problems I want to have. I think most entrepreneurs would purchase that problem as a state. And so, if you're in it, I think, take a deep breath and look at the sunrise or sunset and just enjoy the fact that you've built something that is meaningful enough that people would spend their time. Again, there are amazing snacks that they could be spending the time on otherwise, so that's a huge deal. And then two, you need the art. There's an art and science to picking where to go deep. I will happily respond to folks with, "I really appreciate that. Do you mind sending me a screenshot or a video?" And some of them don't. Okay, that's fine. (00:34:45): You kind of get a sense of quickly looking at how they wrote about it or just pattern matching how detailed they were, or how much they seem that they want to engage and kind of balance it that way. Otherwise, you can tell folks, "This is really awesome. Do you mind sending me an email with three to five bullet points about the details of how you got to this issue?" And that's not a 30-minute meeting. You don't need to blow up your whole life to get on the phone with them. It's not a huge homework assignment to them, but it's enough structure that it will self-select those who want to go deep, and then from there, you really do owe it to them to follow up if they're going to be that detailed. And at that point, you really have made a product friend for life and you'll kind of continuously go back to them. So you have to kind of tune it. (00:35:48): I also will bound some of these efforts, so I'll just completely make up one day a program. So, "Hi, Stripe's doing a bug-finder program." I made that up as I was driving to work one morning, tweeted it, was curious if anyone would send anything. "We'll be taking videos for the next three days to go super deep." And people are like, "Oh my goodness, I would love to be part of the Stripe bug-finder program. May I apply?" I'm like, "Oh, it's very selective. But yes, of course for you." It's just giving people permission through a program, even if it is deeply arbitrary, I find helps with bounding it, and then later I can follow up with the world, "Hey, we ran our first program, we got 65 videos," which we did. "We found dozens of issues," which we did. It was an incredibly valuable use of our time and it really came from just a single tweet.
turns.zh:
我觉得这件事可以分两方面来看。首先，这真是个令人羡慕的难题。在全球所有问题中，“客户兴趣过剩”绝对能跻身我最想遇到的难题之列。我相信大多数创业者都会渴望拥有这样一个难题。既然你正深陷其中，我想你不妨深呼吸一口气，欣赏日出日落，庆幸自己打造出了足以让人们甘愿投入时间的价值所在。毕竟，他们本可以把时间花在其他令人愉悦的零食上——这本身就意义非凡。

其次，你需要掌握“深挖”的艺术。如何精准锁定值得深入探讨的方向，既是科学也是艺术。我通常会回复用户：“非常感谢你的反馈，能否发送截图或视频给我看看？”有时对方未能回应——没关系。（00:34:45）通过快速浏览他们的反馈内容，或是对比他们的详尽程度，能迅速判断对方的诚意。或者你可以这样问：“这想法太棒了！能否用三到五个要点邮件说明你是如何发现这个问题的？”这样既不需要长达30分钟的会议，也不会打扰他们的生活。这对他们来说并非繁琐的任务，但这种结构性引导能自然筛选出真正想深入探讨的用户。此时，你就需要用心跟进。（00:35:48）我还曾尝试通过临时举办活动来规范反馈。比如某天早上开车上班时突发奇想：“Stripe将举办漏洞挖掘活动！未来三天我们将拍摄视频深度探讨。”结果人们疯狂响应：“天哪，我想加入Stripe漏洞挖掘计划！我能申请吗？”我回应：“名额有限，但当然欢迎你。”通过这种看似随意的活动规范流程，之后我向全世界宣布：“我们举办了首期活动，收到65个视频，发现数十个问题。”这真是时间的高效利用，而一切始于一条推文。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Something I saw you mention somewhere is that you only pay attention to feedback from people that are paying customers and ignore everything else. Can you talk about that?
turns.zh: 我记得你在某处提到，你只关注付费用户的反馈，而忽略其他意见。你能谈谈这一点吗？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: People who build things for people tend to be empathetic and interested and curious folks who have friends, and then those friends want to use your stuff because they know you and they like you and they'll have good feedback. But you need to figure out, is that actually your customer, or is that your friend trying it? Who is actually your target customer exactly? Not a company or a segment, not digital natives that are X big. I'm talking about Sarah in this department, who has these tabs open and just faced this problem and needs to solve it by 4:00 PM. That level of specificity. If that's your customer, and I'm talking mostly about B2B, which is where I spend a lot of my time as the social network, B2C stuff I have less intuition on, they're very willing to exchange money for solving their problems, incredibly so. Oftentimes, if you listen with enough silence, they might even say, "I'll pay you money to solve, blah." If you sit there long enough in silence. (00:38:17): And so, you could listen to your friendly friend who you got to play with your beta version and they'll say they liked it and they will click around. But that is extremely different from Sarah, who has the actual problem and is willing to pay. And it is so tempting to go down the first path with the friend group that I sort of needed a rule, which was like, "Okay, rather than..." I was like, "Well, don't pay attention to that quite as much. Really pay attention to, who is your target customer and are you in a fast iteration cycle for them and are they telling their friends?" (00:38:51): But that wasn't enough, because people are so drawn, myself included, drawn to the friendliness that I just set a rule, which is, "We discount all of that feedback from our friends to zero." That is not of interest to us. We don't even write it down. It's just not part of what we're talking about at all. We are only interested in Sarah, our target customer, and can we get her to solve whatever the problem is as quickly as possible, as jangly as possible and go from there? (00:39:26): And then the paying part is a forcing function because again, even with Sarah, because you're paying attention to her and solving her problem a bit, she'll say, "Of course, oh, this is great. I want feature X, Y and Z. Can it do one, two, and three?" Naturally, she would say that. But if you said, "And by the way, this thing is $10,000. We'll happily refund your money 100% the second you don't like it," she might say, "Whoa, whoa, wait a second. Yeah, I like this thing, but not $10, 000. For $10,000, it would need to solve X." And you're like, "Oh, there it is." That was actually what the thing that was of value, and we were all kind of dancing around this. It's useful, we're on the right track, and because I've fallen down that path myself so many times, I just set a rule.
turns.zh: 那些为他人打造产品的人往往富有同理心、兴趣浓厚且好奇心强，他们有朋友支持，而这些朋友因为了解你、喜欢你、会给你好评，所以愿意使用你的产品。但你需要搞清楚，这个人究竟是你的真实客户，还是只是你的朋友在试用？谁才是你的目标客户？不是某个公司或某个细分市场，也不是X大岁的数字原住民。我说的是部门里的莎拉，她打开了多个标签页，刚刚遇到了这个问题，需要在下午四点前解决。这才是具体到客户层面的需求。如果这是你的客户（我主要谈B2B领域，因为我在社交网络公司待得最多，B2C领域我了解得不多），他们非常愿意花钱解决问题，愿意程度超乎想象。很多时候，只要你安静倾听，他们甚至会说：“我愿意花钱让你解决这个问题。”如果你能保持足够的沉默，静静地坐着倾听。（00:38:17） 因此，你可能会倾听那些玩过你的测试版、评价不错的友好朋友的反馈，但这和莎拉完全不同。莎拉才是真正有需求、愿意付费的客户。很想和朋友们一起走第一条路，但我需要给自己定个规矩：“好吧，不要太在意那些反馈。专注于谁是你的目标客户，你们是否在为他们快速迭代，他们是否会向朋友推荐？”（00:38:51） 但这还不够，因为人们，包括我自己，都太容易被友好感所吸引，所以我又定了条规矩：“我们把朋友的反馈归零。”这对我们毫无意义。我们甚至不记录这些反馈。我们只关注目标客户莎拉，能否尽快帮她解决问题，越高效越好？（00:39:26） 然后付费环节就是一个强制函数。即使是莎拉，因为你关注她、为她解决了一些问题，她也会说：“当然，太棒了。我需要功能X、Y和Z。能实现一、二、三吗？”她自然会这么说。但如果你说：“顺便说一句，这个产品要1万美元。一旦你不喜欢，我们会100%退款。”她可能会说：“等等，别急。是的，我喜欢这个产品，但不值1万美元。要1万美元的话，得解决X问题。” 你会说：“哦，原来如此。” 这才是真正有价值的部分，我们之前一直被各种想法绕来绕去。这很有用，我们走对了路，因为我自己也多次走过弯路，所以我定了条规矩。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is great. I was actually going to ask. This technique of using silence, to help people actually practice it, you just shared this quote of, "For you to pay $10,000 it would've to do X." That's a really cool line to use. Is there any other advice there of just how to practice this idea of creating silence to help a potential customer share what they actually need?
turns.zh: 这太棒了。我正想问。这种利用沉默的技巧，帮助人们真正实践它，你刚刚分享了那句话：“要你花1万美元，就得做到X。” 这真是个很棒的台词。有没有其他建议，如何练习这种创造沉默的技巧，帮助潜在客户分享他们的真实需求？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I encourage people to take an improv training class or two, just to get people out of their skin a bit. By the way, this advice applies to big companies also, not just small ones. And we have issues, and I hear other larger companies have issues where a big company will say, "Hey, we're an enterprise and we're going to pay you this big contract. All you need to do is build features one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, and go through security steps, A, B, C, D, E, F, G." And this siren song of the big three-year contract of your first enterprise buyer, even when you're already big, you can go from Fortune 1000 to Fortune 500 to Fortune 10 to Fortune 1. There's always more. There are so many stories of the rug being pulled in the middle and they never actually use it and the contract never lands. (00:41:38): Same in partnerships. And so, I would say the same thing, which is, "If we're super serious about this, send us $1 million. Wire us $1 million. We'll happily wire it back anytime you need it, but let's actually put some stake in the ground about the value." And I find that in the cases in which they're like, "Whoa, wait a second, no, absolutely not. We can't commit here." That's really a good signal because you're about to spend a huge amount of time building something that might not ever be used, and that's the majority case I hear. Or you might get the opposite, which is, "Sounds great. Let's make sure our teams are trained on it faster. How can we get you to our office to explain it? We need it to really work with this system we haven't talked about yet. And now that we're paying, we want it even faster." (00:42:32): And so, I find that it puts a fork in the road towards faster success or avoiding the non-success case. And even at Stripe scale, I've heard our founders somewhat push this methodology on us, where one from the outside might think, "Well, it's a 8,000 person company. Surely they have just regular ways of building things for larger customers, and we too need these style of commitments if we're going to go off roadmap."
turns.zh: 我鼓励大家参加一两节即兴表演培训课程，目的就是让人们能稍微突破自己的舒适区。顺便说一句，这个建议同样适用于大公司，而不只是小企业。我们确实存在一些问题，我听说其他大公司也面临类似困境。比如，大公司会说：“嘿，我们是大型企业，准备给你一份大合同。你们只需开发功能一、二、三、四、五、六、七、八、九，再完成A、B、C、D、E、F、G等安全步骤。”这种大合同的诱惑——比如首个企业客户的三年大合同——即便你已经是大公司，也可能从《财富》1000强企业一路攀升至500强、10强，再到榜首。但欲望永无止境。太多案例中，客户临时反悔，合同最终不了了之。（00:41:38）合作伙伴关系中也存在类似问题。因此，我想强调一点：如果我们对合作足够认真，就直接给他们100万美元。汇款100万美元。我们随时愿意退还，但请先明确价值主张。我发现，当对方说“等等，不行，我们无法承诺”时，这其实是个积极信号，因为你很可能要花大量时间开发一个永远用不上的产品，而这种情况在我听来极为常见。相反，他们也可能说“听起来很棒。我们要尽快培训团队。如何让你们到我们办公室演示？我们需要它与尚未提及的系统集成。既然我们要付钱了，就希望进度更快。”（00:42:32）这些对话决定了项目能否快速成功，或避免失败。即便像Stripe这样的规模大公司，我也听说创始团队会推广这种方法。外界或许会想：“他们可是8000人的公司，肯定有成熟的大客户开发流程吧。”但我们也要明白，如果偏离路线图，同样需要这种承诺机制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So a big lesson you're sharing here is essentially, make sure people are ready to pay for something that they're asking for. That is the ultimate sign that they-
turns.zh: 所以你在这里分享的重要经验是：确保客户准备好为他们要求的服务付费。这是他们真正有需求的最终证明——

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: And by the way, ready to pay is different than paying. Significantly different, significantly different. I've also thought of, "Well, as long as they're ready to pay and they said they would pay and they look at the contract, we should feel good." That is not the same as paying. Paying is an independent group of people saying, "My problem is burning enough that I'm willing to exchange something I have that has value for the promise of what you're going to do." And now it's a real commitment. That is extremely different than ready to. So I will often be on the phone or video, whatever with a founder and I will have them practice charging me. I'll just say, "Hey, I'm just a friend. I'm trying to help you out. It's a little bit self-serving because I work at Stripe and I want to get feedback on our products." (00:44:09): I'll say, "Feel free to sign up for any invoicing or payment service. I don't really care which one. You're welcome to choose Stripe if it's easy enough for you, I'd love to hear your two cents, and send me an invoice or a payment link for $1 right now, right now. That way, when it comes time to actually charge your first customer, it won't be your first time. It won't feel weird. You'll have already done this, you already have a dollar in your account, you already have your logo on the top right of the invoice. It'll feel great." And I probably could go through my email inbox and just see $1 receipts to random people because I'm just so convinced that the difference between paying and willing, ready, I thought they would pay is night and day different.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，"准备好付款"和"实际付款"是两回事。天壤之别。我曾想过："只要他们准备好付款，签了合同，我们就该满意了。"但这和实际付款完全不是一回事。付款意味着一群独立的人说："我的问题是迫切需要把有价值的东西换成对方的承诺。"这才是真正的承诺。这和"准备好付款"完全不同。所以我经常和创始人通电话或开视频会议，让他们模拟给我收费。我会说："嘿，我只是个朋友。我想帮你一把。这有点自私，因为我在Stripe工作，想听听你们对我们产品的反馈。"（00:44:09）我会说："随意注册任何发票或支付服务吧。我不在乎选哪个。如果Stripe对你们来说够简单，欢迎用它。我很想听听你们的看法。现在就给我发送1美元的发票或支付链接。这样等你们真正给第一个客户收费时，就不会手足无措了。不会觉得别扭。你们已经做过一次了，账户里已经有1美元，发票上还有你们的Logo。这感觉棒极了。"我甚至能翻看我的邮箱，找到给陌生人的1美元收据，因为我深信付款和"准备好付款"、"愿意付款"的区别天差地别。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, there's this term, willingness to pay that I feel like it should change, as you're saying, to just cross that willingness to even just-
turns.zh: 是啊，有个术语叫"愿意付款"，我觉得应该改成"付款意愿"，这样更准确。就是要跨过那个"愿意付款"的阶段——

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Paying.
turns.zh: 付款。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Paying, exactly.
turns.zh: 付款，准确来说。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Yeah. And we can refund the money. There's no issue at all. Just other tricks on how to get people going is, ask them about their regular life as a human, "What did you do yesterday?" And they'll be like, "Oh, at work?" I'm like, "Or not. Whatever." And people, they'll start to spill, they'll just start to spill and eventually they'll get to their biggest problem pretty quickly.
turns.zh: 是的。我们可以退款。完全没问题。还有其他让人们行动起来的技巧，比如问他们日常生活："昨天做了什么？"他们会说："哦，工作啊？"我会说："或者不是。随便啦。" 这样一来，人们就会打开话匣子，很快就能聊到他们最大的难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about metrics, going in a different direction. Many people told me I need to ask you about picking metrics and the importance of metrics and how you think about metrics. So let me just maybe start with a question of, just why do you think picking the right metric and why are metrics so important in building successful products?
turns.zh: 我们来谈谈指标，换个话题。很多人让我问你关于指标选择、指标重要性以及如何看待指标的问题。那么我或许可以从一个问题开始：为什么你认为选择正确的指标如此重要？为什么指标对打造成功产品如此关键？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I somewhat walk around with the belief that the product manager's responsibility is to produce product market fit. And okay, how do you know you have product market fit? Charts that showcase things are going up into the right on one hand, and then tweets on the other. So metrics like quantitative and qualitative, and I really see them as deep siblings and equals, you really need both. It's not oh, OKRs versus something. There are some things you want the texture of the person on video showing how complicated a thing was. And then also, we're trying to make an economically viable system that we can run at large scale and you can't keep all that stuff in your head and need to measure it. And so, I think metrics at their best are a numerical representation of the value we're providing for the customer. (00:46:59): One could measure anything. You can just start counting events and log lines. We've made it incredibly cheap to count stuff. And so, now we have this big privilege of choosing what to measure. And I really just try to map it all the way back to, "Well, what was actually the value that we're trying to produce for the customer and can we measure it from their perspective?" Whereas I think it's natural, both because when you work inside of a company, you're just thinking internally, but also the way that the metrics are collected inside your application to be more internal-oriented. How many people logged in? Okay, that's a fine measure, but how many people accomplished what they were trying to do after they logged in, is not just necessarily sitting there as a single event in your database. You have to think about it a bit. Another reason why I spend a lot of time crafting a small number of these metrics is, they force trade-offs and decisions. (00:47:56): So we could all sit around all day and say, "Hey, I heard all these customer problems, we should build X, Y, and Z." And another person could absolutely reasonably say, "Well, I heard from these customers, we should build one, two and three." And they're all true. We could have a lot of success in both, but the majority case is that we don't build either and we sit around and argue and bicker and we go slowly. "What are we going to do to naturally, organically every day, orient a larger group of people in the right direction and see if our tactics are generating progress over time for a customer from their perspective?" And metrics on the left and a series of tweets on the right is a pretty great combo. (00:48:42): Here's an example. A couple years ago I had been working in our payments group at Stripe for a bit, and then I started working on some of our banking and incorporation services. In Atlas, when I started working on it, it had had some success. It had already existed for four or five years prior to me spending time on it. But when I started to look at the support tickets, people were pretty unhappy frequently. They had a DocuSign stuck in their email box. They needed a co-founder's address, but they didn't know their co-founder's address. They couldn't log into the dashboard to figure out their 83(b) manual filing instructions. And we saw this basically in the first week of spending time on Atlas. I was just like, "Just show me all the support tickets. Are they happy support tickets? People writing in being like, 'Oh, I love this service, it's absolutely fantastic. Can you just do A, B, C more for me?' Or are they sad support tickets?" And they're like, "Oh my God, they're all sad support tickets." (00:49:45): And so, we're just asking ourselves, "Well, why would someone recommend Atlas to a friend?" I was like, "Well, it would have to accomplish A, B and C activities for them. It would have to get their company, it would have to handle getting their tax ID from the IRS. It'd have to handle all the downstream administrivia." But surely, if they had a bunch of support tickets at the end, they're not going to go tell their friends to use this thing. We could measure all of the intermediate parts, we could measure the success rate and the frequency of incorporation services and we do all those things, but if you looked at the support tickets, there's just no way if you had a support ticket, you would recommend it to a friend. And so, we suggested this metric to ourselves, companies that have no support tickets through the incorporation service. (00:50:36): The whole process, from the moment you start the application open, actually the first page load at the very beginning, all the way through the process waiting for the government, waiting for the IRS, and we give you two more weeks to write into support. We give an extra buffer two weeks. And if you get through that whole thing with no support tickets, that's a yes. If you have any number of support tickets, that's a no. And we just looked at the percentage of founders that were going through the service with zero support tickets, which is very different than looking at an average, right? You could have the average as 0.3, but that doesn't necessarily mean that they're getting to 0.2 is going to cause them to tell their friends more. And we looked, and only 15% of founders were getting through Atlas with zero support tickets through that metric. (00:51:31): And I just thought, "Okay, well let's just drive that number way up, and let's look at the support tickets aside what people are needing and we'll bake it into the product, and presumably it'll fix it. People will like that more and then tell their friends." And over about 18 months, we took that number from 15% to 85. We basically just flipped it. And you can look at the market share plotted on the same timeframe and it's the same shape. And I think you have to find a measure by which it speaks directly to what the customer wanted, and that if you accidentally leaked your dashboard to them, your customer would be ecstatic to learn that that's what you were measuring the whole time. If we were to showcase the internal Atlas metrics, which we often just screenshot and publish, I think they'd be pretty happy to hear that we were spending all of our time making sure that none of them had support tickets. (00:52:33): And it was incredibly encouraging and motivating to the engineers on the team because we could just assign them a topic. "Hey, look at all these support tickets. Why don't you come up with the product spec, the scope, the solution? Oh, want to learn more? Just reply to the support ticket email, figure out what they need." And so, we kind of turned all of the engineers on the team into PMs to go and one issue at a time, figure out what needed to change and build products for it. And that's where we pushed forward on 83(b) elections, automating it, sending in the mail for folks. We built our own signing service. (00:53:17): We turned everything into a click. We did just did sort of the obvious things we saw in the tickets, but as the PM, I was able to just sort of, not on autopilot, but really sit back and have content full conversations with engineers who were bringing solutions and ideas for product, rather than one person going through all of the potential ideas, scoping them and assigning them. And because it was based in what people were saying and wanted, it was very motivating for everyone on the team. So somewhat long answer, but figuring out something in which every day we can wake up and look at the same metric and with some confidence know what to do, is so much better than, "Let's figure out what to do each month, and starting from scratch."
turns.zh:
我多少有点秉持这样的观点：产品经理的职责是实现产品与市场的适配。那么，如何判断产品是否达到了市场适配呢？一方面是图表上数据不断攀升，另一方面是社交媒体上的推文反馈。量化指标和定性反馈本质上是相辅相成的，两者缺一不可。这不是二选一的问题。比如，用户视频中展示的复杂流程，远比单纯的OKR更能传递价值。同时，我们要打造一个经济可行的系统，支持大规模运营——所有这些信息都不能仅停留在脑海中，必须通过数据来量化。

（00:46:59）：任何事物都可以被量化。你可以开始记录事件和日志行。我们现在获取数据的成本已经极低，因此可以自由选择要追踪的指标。我始终追溯到一个核心问题：我们为客户创造了怎样的价值？能否从他们的视角去衡量？相反，许多人在公司内部工作时，往往只关注内部视角，而应用程序中的数据收集也更偏向内部导向。例如，多少用户登录了？这固然是不错的指标，但登录后完成目标的用户数量却不一定能直接从数据库中获取。这需要深思熟虑。正因如此，我花大量时间打磨少数关键指标——它们迫使我们在取舍中做出决策。

（00:47:56）：如果我们整天坐在一起说：“嘿，我听说了这些客户问题，我们应该开发X、Y和Z。”另一个人完全可以合理地反驳：“嗯，我也听说了这些客户需求，我们应该做一、二、三。”两种方案都可能成功，但多数情况下，我们最终既不实施其中任何一个方案，又陷入无休止的争执和拖延。关键问题在于：我们如何自然、渐进地引导更大规模的团队朝着正确方向前进，并从客户视角观察策略是否在逐步创造价值？左边的图表和右边的一系列推文，这是一个绝佳组合。

（00:48:42）：举个例子。几年前，我在Stripe的支付团队工作了一段时间后，开始参与我们的银行和公司注册服务。在Atlas上，我刚开始参与时它已经取得了一定的成功。在我加入之前，它已经存在了四五年。但当我开始查看支持票时，用户频繁抱怨。他们邮箱里有卡在处理的DocuSign文档。他们需要联合创始人的地址，却不知道对方的邮箱。无法登录仪表板去查找83(b)手动申报指南。这些问题在我们刚接触Atlas的第一周就暴露无遗。我就问：“把所有支持票都给我看看。都是满意的吗？用户写着‘哦，我爱死这项服务了，简直太棒了。能不能帮我多做A、B、C这些事？’还是都是不满的反馈？”结果发现，全是用户的抱怨。

（00:49:45）：于是我们自问：为什么用户会不满？
有人向朋友推荐Atlas吗？我当时想，"嗯，它得帮他们完成A、B和C这些任务。得帮他们注册公司，处理从美国国税局获取税务识别号的流程，还要处理后续的行政琐事。"但说真的，如果最后用户留下一堆支持票，他们肯定不会去推荐这个工具。我们可以衡量中间各个环节的成功率和注册服务的频率，我们也确实做了这些统计，但如果你看看支持票数据，用户如果有支持票，就绝对不会推荐给朋友。所以我们为自己设定了一个指标——那些通过Atlas注册服务且没有产生任何支持票的公司。（00:50:36）：整个流程从开始申请那一刻起，第一页加载到最后，再到等待政府审批、等待国税局回复的整个过程，我们还额外给两周时间让用户反馈问题。我们给出了两个星期的缓冲期。如果整个流程下来没有产生任何支持票，那就是成功。如果有任何支持票，那就是失败。我们统计了通过Atlas注册服务且没有产生任何支持票的创始人比例，这和看平均值很不一样，对吧？平均值可能是0.3，但这并不意味着他们得到0.2就会更愿意推荐朋友。我们发现，只有15%的创始人通过这个指标顺利完成注册。（00:51:31）：我当时就想，"好吧，那我们就把这个数字大幅提升，让支持票数据与用户实际需求脱钩，融入产品设计，这样用户应该更满意，也更愿意推荐。"在大约18个月里，我们把这个比例从15%提升到85%。基本上实现了翻倍。你可以看看同期市场份额曲线图，形状是一样的。我认为衡量标准必须直接对应客户需求，如果你不小心向他们透露了仪表板，他们会欣喜若狂地发现你一直在衡量这些数据。如果我们展示Atlas的内部指标（我们经常截图发布），他们应该会很高兴听到我们把所有精力都投入到确保用户没有支持票上。（00:52:33）：这对团队工程师来说非常鼓舞人心、富有激励性，因为我们可以直接分配给他们一个任务："看看这些支持票吧。你能不能制定产品规范、范围和解决方案？哦，想了解更多？回复支持票邮件，搞清楚用户需求。"这样，我们就把团队所有工程师都转化为产品经理，让他们一次解决一个问题，确定需要改进的地方并开发产品。正因如此，我们推进了83(b)选举自动化，为用户邮寄材料。我们还开发了自己的签名服务（00:53:17）。我们把所有流程都简化为一键操作。我们只是处理了支持票中显而易见的问题，但作为产品经理，我能够不依赖自动化，而是真正与工程师坐下来深入探讨产品解决方案，而不是让一个人筛选所有可能的想法、评估范围和
分配任务给他们。由于这个决策是基于大家的意见和需求做出的,所以对团队里的每个人来说都很有激励作用。所以虽然回答有点长，但找到一个方法，让我们每天醒来后都能查看同样的数据指标，并且能比较有信心地知道接下来该做什么，这比起"每个月都从零开始思考该做什么"要好得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think this is amazing and important advice, just the power of a single metric that everyone on the team can understand, rally around and use to prioritize the work they're doing. I've seen exactly the same sort of impact. Funny enough, Airbnb, one of the teams actually had a metric sort of like this, basically reducing the people contacting Airbnb with support issues. But what ended up happening is, their team started just making it harder to contact support because they're like, "Maybe they don't need to contact support about all these trivial issues, so maybe let's encourage them to figure it out themselves." Is there anything you've learned about to try to avoid these kind of second order effects that are of perverse incentives of a metric?
turns.zh: 我认为这条建议既令人惊叹又极具价值——只需制定一个团队成员都能理解、共同认可并用于工作优先级排序的核心指标，就能产生巨大影响。我亲眼见证过类似的效果。说来有趣，Airbnb团队就曾制定过类似的指标，成功减少了用户因支持问题联系客服的次数。但最终的结果是，团队反而让用户更难联系客服支持，因为他们认为："用户没必要为这些琐碎问题反复求助，或许我们应该引导他们自己解决问题。"对于如何避免因指标设计引发的反向激励效应，大家有什么经验值得分享吗？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: We look at multiple metrics, but we will optimize around one and you have to use your own judgment to look at some of these countermeasures and pick them. We would also, that would sort of be our overarching metric for a year, but then we would pick specific tactical metrics about how we would accomplish it. So just an example that both is how we solved a problem, but also it's just a style of metric that was useful to us. Of course, some of these support tickets included things like, "I'm waiting to hear back from Atlas about, if they're going to approve my application because Stripe is required for very good reasons to evaluate certain business types, or sanctions, lists and the worldwide products." So there is some, should be incredibly quick, but there is a bit of a review process, and of course if you were not hearing back from us, you would be upset because you're trying to make your company immediately, "This is ridiculous. Let's get back to us quickly." (00:55:59): And so, we knew that one of the reasons that people were writing to support was like, "Hey, what's up with my review? What's going on?" And we knew that our tactic was just to drive up how quickly we got to a final decision on folks and to reduce the number of overturned rejections, where someone writes back in saying, "Hi, come on, I'm totally just making something reasonable. What's up? Why did you reject me?" And so, we would pick these overarching single metric, which was the companies with zero support tickets, but then we would have a specific KR that was owned by an engineer, which is the tactic that we're going to do. And so, we would not allow ourselves the perverse tactics to sort of just casually exist. We would choose which tactics we're going to do and then set a metric for it. (00:56:49): And the other reason I love this metric is, it's a cohort metric by which you're trying to drive something up into the left. Sometimes people will get excited about a chart that goes up into the right, it's kind of a meme, "Oh, that's going up to the right." I'm really excited about charts that go up into the left. So you have to figure out some optimization that you're trying to maximize. And so, in this particular case of this risk review, we would look at, "Hey, for the cohort of customers that started last month, how quickly did we get them to their final risk review by number of days since they submitted?" And so, you want a chart that looks a lot like, "Here we go, right up to the top." Because you want 100% of your customers to get their final decision as quickly as possible. (00:57:44): Wouldn't you know it, when we looked at the chart, it was doing this. And so, each month we would just make it a little better, a little better, a little up and to the left, up and to the left, up and to the left. And now basically 100-ish percent of people get their risk review within an hour, from a long tail taking a long time. And so, we would constrain the tactic through a metric and then watch it through an optimization function. And then when we got to a point where we were happy with the target, we could put down the tactic. That's another really useful thing about metrics, you can decide when to stop a tactic because you get to some level of success that you're comfortable with and you can always choose to pick it back up later.
turns.zh:
我们会综合多个指标，但会重点围绕一个核心指标进行优化。您需要凭借自身判断，审视这些优化措施并加以选择。当然，这一年我们的总体指标可能会有所调整，但具体战术指标将围绕如何达成目标而制定。举个例子，当我们解决某个问题时，会采用某种指标衡量其效果，而这种指标风格对我们而言十分有效。  

有些支持工单的内容涉及复杂问题，如“我正在等待Atlas的审批结果，因为Stripe出于合理原因需要评估特定业务类型、制裁名单及全球产品”。此类情况本应迅速处理，但审批流程仍存在一定延迟。若用户长时间未收到回复，难免会感到不满：“这也太慢了吧，赶紧给个回复！”  

我们发现，用户咨询的主要原因在于：“我的审批进度如何？到底怎么回事？”我们的策略是加快最终决策速度，减少被推翻的拒绝案例。例如，有用户反驳道：“我只是合理申请，怎么会被拒？”针对这些问题，我们设定了一个核心指标——“零支持工单率”，同时由工程师负责制定具体的关键绩效指标（KR）并执行策略。我们坚决摒弃那些无效的权宜之计，选择经过深思熟虑的优化方案。  

另一个让我青睐的指标是队列分析。有些人会对向右攀升的图表兴奋不已，但我更关注向左攀升的曲线。当看到客户群体的风险审批速度不断提升时，我们欣喜不已。例如，我们会追踪上月新注册客户的审批时长，将其与提交后的天数进行对比，目标是让所有客户在一小时内完成风险评估。  

令人惊喜的是，通过持续优化，90%左右的用户现在都能在一小时内完成审批。这一成果充分证明了指标驱动策略的有效性，让我们在达成目标后果断终止无效措施。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So there's some really cool lessons here of just how to pick a good metric. Just to kind of maybe summarize what I'm hearing is, you kind of worked backwards from essentially NPS, like, "Why aren't people recommending Atlas?" You found, "Okay, well people that are complaining and having issues with support and running into problems, most likely are going to be detractors, not going to want to recommend Atlas, so let's have those really ambitious goals. Eventually nobody has a support ticket/let's just track how many people have zero issues." And then you identify, "Okay, what's driving a lot of these support tickets? It looks like this risk timeline till they get to this certain milestone, let's make that our goal for the next quarter or whatever, and let's focus there and then make an impact." And then I imagine move on to other levers within this bucket of zero context.
turns.zh: 接下来，这里有一些关于如何选择合适指标的绝佳经验之谈。简而言之，关键在于从NPS（客户净推荐值）这样的指标逆向推导。比如，"为什么人们不推荐Atlas？"你会发现，那些抱怨服务、遇到支持问题或遇到故障的用户很可能是负面口碑来源，不太可能推荐Atlas，所以你需要设定高远目标。比如，"最终没人提交支持工单"，或者"只追踪零问题用户的数量"。然后你会思考，"是什么导致了大量支持工单？"看起来是用户在达到某个里程碑前的风险期，这可以成为下一季度的工作重点，专注于此并产生影响。之后，我猜你会转向其他零上下文领域的优化措施。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: You have to pick the right metric for your audience in... I wouldn't wouldn't fully export that metric to everyone. That was not a terrible one to export, but in the founders choosing where to get started mindset, again, this isn't just deeply spending time listening to your customers. They all ask their friends, "Hey, how did you start your company?" They want to talk to an older sibling of sorts about how it went. And so, we decided that our go-to-market strategy would be to delight our current customers such that they would tell their friends. And other businesses, that's always somewhat useful, but you can also reach people with billboards and Google ads and other types of upsells. That's very difficult in the moment that someone is starting a company that's sort of a National Geographic, can you get the picture of the bird at exactly the right time? (01:00:10): How are you even supposed to go find people who are about to start companies? Thankfully, they have this practice of just asking their friends. And so, if their friends loved it, they're going to just recommend it. And that has the metric and the tactic and the go-to-market all lined up, rather than sometimes in cases you might hear someone say, "Well, let's make the product quality better." Well, we all make the product quality better, but why? Why is this actually going to move what our customers want, and the business board? And when you can line them all up, it can be quite beautiful, especially when you can see it month-over-month for a long period of time. One other metric I think that I would export to anybody, is if you are unsure what to measure, we have this, I don't know if we stole it from somebody else or if we came up with internally, whatever, is just users having a bad day, where we will just emit a log line anytime we think that a user bumped into a problem. (01:01:14): So maybe they hit a 404, or maybe their payout was one day after the ETA, or they had more than 10 payment declines, you can kind of brainstorm again or just listen to customers, what would cause you to personally have a bad day, and then just emit an event when that occurs. And then you could just make a stacked bar chart of all the bad day reasons and the frequency by which they're happening, and it's eye-opening to see those frequencies. And it's kind of a metric I hadn't thought about until Stripe's scale, in which you just don't know what's happening until you emit the log line and count it. The frequencies could be...
turns.zh: 你必须为目标受众选择合适的指标……我不建议将某个指标一股脑推广给所有人。推广某个指标本质上没错，但对于初创公司创始人来说，他们往往没有深入倾听客户需求的耐心。他们会问朋友："你是怎么创办公司的？"想向"前辈"取经。所以我们决定，市场推广策略应以满足现有客户需求为核心，让他们主动推荐给朋友。这在某种程度上是有用的，但初创公司也可能通过广告牌、谷歌广告等方式推广客户。但当你面对一个像《国家地理》般宏大的初创公司时，很难精准捕捉用户行为的关键瞬间。（01:00:10）：你如何找到即将创业的人？幸运的是，他们会向朋友求助。如果朋友喜欢你的产品，他们自然会推荐。这就让指标、策略和市场推广完美对接了。而有时你会听到有人说："那我们就提高产品质量吧。"但提高产品质量容易，但为什么要这么做？这对客户需求和商业目标有何实际意义？当所有环节都协调一致时，效果会显著得多，尤其是当你能长期追踪月度数据时。另一个我认为值得推广的指标是——如果你不确定该衡量什么，我们开发了这样一个指标（不知道是借鉴他人还是内部研发），就是"用户糟糕的一天"。每当用户遇到问题时，我们就会记录日志。比如404错误、付款延迟一天、支付失败超过10次等。这能让你重新审视用户可能遇到的糟糕体验，然后在这些情况发生时触发事件。接着你可以制作一个堆积柱状图，展示各种糟糕体验的原因和发生频率，数据令人震惊。这种指标在Stripe这样的规模公司之前可能没人想到过——直到你开始记录并统计数据后，才会发现问题的严重性。这些频率数据可能……

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: ... emit the log line and count it. The frequencies could be kind of mind-blowing. And I think for almost any scale business, if you are bored one day and you're not sure what to measure, just make a user having a bad day chart, emit a log line and count it as a bar chart and then anybody else can add their own bar chart on top of it. And so, it's become a way for teams to scale their understanding of users through metrics by just saying, "Hey, look, anytime anybody has an idea about why a customer is having a bad day, just emit a log line, put it on this chart, and then we can choose over time which bad day reasons we want to burn down and hopefully just eradicate them, not just minimize them. (01:02:41): But it gave us kind of a background noise counting system for where there are problems and anytime there's an incident or some customer issue, the first thing I think is, "Ooh, I wonder if we have a bad day reason for this." And if we do, I actually feel okay. I'm like, "Oh yeah, it is a bad day for this customer." I wish I didn't have it, but at least we're aware and we can evaluate it against other bad days that we want to burn down. What does sometimes a little bit grind my gears or gives us an opportunity is like when we didn't know about that bad day. And it's a surprise to us too, that is for me is immediate action. It's like, okay, cool. We have to figure out a way to count this bad day. We got to get it on the chart. That way we can make an informed decision about when to invest improving it.
turns.zh: ……输出日志记录并进行统计。这些频率可能会令人震惊。我认为对于几乎任何规模的企业来说，如果你某天无聊且不知道该衡量什么数据时，只需创建一个“用户糟糕体验日”的图表，输出日志记录并将其以柱状图呈现，随后其他人可以在此基础上添加自己的柱状图。这已成为团队通过数据洞察用户行为的有效方式——只需说：“嘿，看看，每当有人对用户为何会度过糟糕的一天感到困惑时，就输出日志记录并添加到图表中，然后我们可以逐步分析并消除这些导致用户体验不佳的因素，而非仅仅是减少其发生频率。”（01:02:41）但这为我们提供了一个持续监测问题根源的背景数据系统。每当出现事故或客户问题时，首先想到的可能是：“哦，用户今天遇到的问题是否与某个糟糕体验日相关？”如果确实如此，我会觉得这很正常。会想：“没错，用户今天确实遇到了糟糕体验。” 我希望这样的情况不会发生，但至少我们能意识到问题，并与其他需要改进的糟糕体验日进行对比。偶尔遇到未曾预料到的糟糕体验日时，比如当我们对其毫无准备时，那才是真正需要立即行动的时候。比如，我们必须想办法统计这种糟糕体验，将其添加到图表中，从而为改进工作提供依据。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I love this idea. I haven't heard this before. So the idea is just make a list of what happens to a potential customer that would cause them to have a bad day. What are some examples for Striper Atlas that you guys have?
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这个想法。之前从未听说过。核心思路就是列出可能导致潜在客户产生糟糕体验的因素。针对 Stripe Atlas，你们有什么具体案例吗？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Are you a Stripe customer, Lenny?
turns.zh: Lenny，你是 Stripe 的客户吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I am with my newsletters. The payments go through Stripe. I check my dashboard every day.
turns.zh: 我是，订阅了他们的通讯服务。支付通过 Stripe 处理，我每天都会查看仪表板。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Cool. So what would be a bad day for you?
turns.zh: 不错。那对你来说，什么样的情况算糟糕体验日？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, I see some silence happening here. It not loading. The numbers taking a long time to show up. Something being completely off in there, not being able to log in. The silence is good. I just want to keep going.
turns.zh: 哦，我看到这边有点卡顿。数据加载太慢，图表迟迟不显示。可能后台出了问题，登录不了。没关系，我继续。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: The question is how much to the audience is how much of the silence will we edit out before it goes live? But this is what I'm talking about, right, is I could guess them, right? And as you were saying those, I know the URL of those charts. I know the login one because I feel that too. So I play with Stripe all the time and then you get a two FA too frequently and come on, I had the same cookie. I was just here yesterday. So we count all that stuff and try to make it better over time. But I'm so excited when someone brings me a new bad day I hadn't thought about yet because that's like product cabinet.
turns.zh: 问题是，观众希望我们在直播前剪掉多少这类无声片段？但这就是我要说的重点，对吧？我能猜到这些问题，对吧？你列举这些例子时，我知道这些图表的网址。登录那部分我也感同身受。我经常玩 Stripe ，但有时也会遇到两次失败登录，拜托，我用的还是同一个 Cookie，昨天才登录过。所以我们会统计所有这些问题，逐步改进。但当有人给我带来一个我从未想到过的糟糕体验日时，我会特别兴奋，因为这就像产品创新库。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. And your advice here is this doesn't necessarily have to be your goal or metric. It's just watching this thing that could lead to a lot of interesting ways of operating.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个了。你的建议是，这不一定非得是你的目标或衡量指标。关键是观察这些可能引发许多有趣运营方式的数据。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: A couple other just like quick metrics things because it's a bit of a... I don't know, some people like cycling or something. I guess, I like metrics. People get a really nice bike. I want a really great metric. Picking metric titles that make you feel something. So we could have called that measure of companies, number of companies that do not send a support ticket over X period and Y period with min... You sometimes see these charts where the metric itself named itself. This is just companies with zero support, that's it. And the brevity and the focus and the customer mindset built into the chart name can become currency inside the company. It's like, oh, I'm working on making this chart go up and it feels good to just say the name out loud rather than some complicated underscores and mins and maxes and the database field name is still in the chart title. (01:06:26): These are aesthetic choices, but I think make dramatic differences in the cultural willingness for people to buy in and get excited about it and reduce the need of a product person to just remind everyone every day why they're doing it. It's like the metric is motivating us because it's a motivating thing to talk about. And then lastly on metrics is there's just good hygiene that people should bring to their measures. Percentages shouldn't have 41 significant digits if only two of the digits are relevant. You should keep all the measures of your dashboard on the same X-axis. These are just stylistic things that increase the frequency that people want to just wake up every day and open the dashboard and look at it. And that is so powerful if your whole team is looking at the same set of information that has the heartbeat of the customer every single day. (01:07:26): In fact, we can measure at Stripe the usage of our dashboards by team, and so we can see which teams are themselves looking at their own metrics and that is an incredibly useful predictor of how on the same page they are and how customer obsessed they are. So I just think it's not an area that's sort of behind the scenes, bean counting reliability is the machine hot. You can make metrics that mean something to the customer and you would be proud if they were to be screenshot and put on the internet and be like, "Wow, I feel like that company is taking their promise to me seriously. And I can see myself on those metrics as a customer." That's where we're really shooting for.
turns.zh:
还有几个关于指标的小细节，因为这有点……我不知道，有些人喜欢骑自行车之类的。我猜，我喜欢指标。人们会买一辆很棒的自行车，而我想要一个非常出色的指标。选择能激发情感的指标标题。比如，我们本可以给这个指标起个名字，比如“在X段时间和Y段时间内未提交支持工单的公司数量”，但用了简洁的表达……有时候你会看到一些图表，指标名称本身就很直观。这就是零支持率的公司，仅此而已。图表名称中内含的简洁性、专注性和客户思维，往往能在公司内部形成一种共鸣。比如，“哦，我正在努力让这个图表上升”，光是大声说出这个名字就感觉很棒，而不是那些复杂的下划线、最小值和最大值，而且数据库字段名称仍然保留在图表标题中。

（01:06:26）：这些都是美学选择，但我认为它们对激发员工的参与度和热情有着显著的影响，也能减少产品团队每天提醒大家为何要做这些工作的必要性。指标本身就能激励我们，因为谈论它是一种激励人心的方式。最后，关于指标，还有一些基本的规范需要注意。比如，如果只有两位数是相关的，百分比就不应该有41位小数。仪表板的所有指标都应该使用相同的X轴。这些都是提升用户体验的细节，让人们每天醒来后都愿意打开仪表板查看数据。如果整个团队每天都在关注与客户息息相关的信息，这其中的影响力是巨大的。

（01:07:26）：事实上，我们在Stripe可以按团队衡量仪表板的使用情况，这样就能看到哪些团队会主动查看自己的指标。这是判断他们是否步调一致、是否以客户为中心的极佳指标。所以我认为这不是什么幕后、枯燥的数据统计，而是实实在在能让客户感知到公司的用心的关键。让指标对客户有意义，让他们截图分享到网上并感叹“哇，我感觉这家公司真的在认真履行对我的承诺。作为客户，我能从这些指标中看到自己的存在感。”这才是我们的最终目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So [inaudible 01:08:19] back what you just said there, which I think is a subtle point potentially, is just making the dashboard look nice, like the hygiene of the naming conventions and the decimal points and the chart. In your experience, you find that really powerful and important.
turns.zh: 所以[听不清 01:08:19]回到你刚才说的，这可能是个微妙的观点，那就是让仪表板看起来美观，比如命名规范、数字格式和图表设计。根据你的经验，你发现这真的很强大且重要。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: A couple of years ago, Stripe did internal work to make an internal metrics kind of dashboard system. And we have a special place called Go Metrics. Many people use a go/service where you can just quickly go to a URL. And again, I have to sometimes do a rule rather than a policy. My rule is if it's not on Go Metrics, I'm not going to look at it. So if people can send me one-off queries or charts or screenshots or presentations or emails of charts and data, but that is in the wind, we can't interrogate the query metrics are almost always wrong. For many weeks, we didn't quite get the definition correctly. You have to live in the metric for quite a while before you really believe in it. And so, if you're always looking at some one-off version, it's just very difficult for it to rise up to the level of importance that is a thing we should trust to help us decide what to do. That's an incredibly high bar. And so, I just find you have to look at it frequently enough. (01:09:46): And if you're going to look at it frequently enough, it means it needs to be in a discoverable place. You almost go through a couple stages of grief about it because we'll kind of put a metric up in a place and everyone initially is like, "Wow, this is great. I was so excited to finally see this." And then a couple of days later, "I don't quite understand it. What does it actually mean? I saw this other metric from this other angle that kind of makes it feel counterintuitive that it's like this." And then you kind of look into it, "Wait a second, we've been counting it wrong the whole time. Oh, no." And then you look at it the third week and it's a completely different version and then you hope that we forget about it and maybe we'll go onto something else and nope, we're not going to forget about it. Week four comes around, you're like, "Wait a second. Okay, this is..." Then the team meeting starts, "Hey, just a reminder, let's just bring up the metric again, not a screenshot of it. Go to the URL." (01:10:39): And just that level of frequency and specificity and ritual around it is what brings it into the decision-making culture. And again, we treat it the exact same as we do tweets. It's the quantitative and qualitative right next to each other. And because you're putting that amount of attention to it, you can't have a 1,000 metrics. We just don't physically have time the day to bring that level of care and understanding to so many things. So then it forces you to know so many things you could care about down to a small number of things that you really must care about. And again, that practice goes back to do you really understand what your customer wants? And so, for all these tactics, it's about finding out what your customer wants and then different versions of how do we sort of know it's true over time and our tactics improving?
turns.zh:
几年前，Stripe内部开发了一个用于监控指标的仪表板系统，我们称之为Go Metrics。许多人会使用Go/Service平台，只需快速访问一个网址即可。但有时我不得不采取规则而非政策的手段。我的原则是，如果某项数据不在Go Metrics平台上，我绝不会去查看它。因此，即便有人发送一次性查询、图表、截图、演示文稿或数据邮件，我们也无法对其进行深入分析——这些数据往往存在严重错误。数周以来，我们始终未能正确理解指标定义。只有在亲身实践并反复验证后，才能真正认可其价值。若始终只能看到零星数据，根本无法将其提升至足以影响决策的层级。这门槛实在太高。因此，我认为必须让指标足够易于获取。

（01:09:46）：若要频繁查看指标，就必须将其置于易于发现的位置。人们往往会经历一个痛苦的适应过程：刚开始将指标上线时，大家兴奋不已，感叹"太棒了，终于能看到这些数据了！"。但几天后又困惑不已："这到底什么意思？我看到的另一个角度数据完全相反，感觉根本说不通啊！"然后深入研究发现："天哪，我们整个过程中都算错了！"

（01:10:39）：第四周重新审视时，指标版本已完全不同。团队会议上，人们再次提醒："别发截图了，直接访问网址！"。正是这种频繁性、精准性和仪式感，才能将指标融入决策文化。正如我们对待推特消息一样，将定量与定性数据并行呈现。正因如此，我们无法同时管理上千个指标——毕竟每天精力有限，无法为如此多数据投入同等的关注。因此，必须将关注点集中于少数关键指标。这又回归到核心问题：你是否真正理解客户需求？所有策略的核心都是：找到客户真正想要的，并通过不同版本的数据验证其真实性，持续优化策略。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It sounds so simple when you describe it that way. This episode is brought to you by Anvil. Their document SDK helps product teams build and launch software for documents fast.
