turns.en: Okay, sounds like we're close.
turns.zh: 好的，看来我们已经很接近目标了。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: We're on our way.
turns.zh: 我们正在稳步推进。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Sounds like we're close. The other stat I have here is that the fastest growing cities for startups. Here's what I have, I don't know if you know this, but Boulder, Shenzhen, and Las Vegas.
turns.zh: 听起来我们确实快成功了。我这里还有另一项数据，关于初创企业最快速发展的城市。不知道你们是否了解，但榜上有名的是博尔德、深圳和拉斯维加斯。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: They're everywhere. One of the, it's like stat we kind of came up with a little bit last year that I'm just personally deeply obsessed with is founding teams in which the co-founders are in multiple countries. So we kind of nickname this. Again, it's like giving things a good title, headlines. Cross-Border Founders. Wow. More than 20% of multi-founder teams have at least one founder from another country. That is astounding to me, that the internet could bring people together like that. And I think that's going to provide more perspectives, more solutions will be local and global. Just all perspectives are great. And again, I think the Atlas team itself represents this. We were very intentional of how we built the Atlas team. It's majority women and we have more diversity to hire, but we're just very intentional to make it a team that had diverse perspectives. You've been on teams that don't have diverse perspectives of any type. They are so much worse. There's no real science necessary here. We just enforce that. We had the opportunity to build this team that way. (01:56:36): And it was really important to me that it represented a world we wanted things to look like and to represent. And it just had to be very intentional about it because I've made mistakes in my career previously where my startup was all men when we sold to box one of them. And on each hire it was harder and harder and harder to hire someone of a different background. Just naturally folks didn't want to join that type of team. And that was the last time I've ever going to make that mistake, which is that early the candidate poll must match where you want the team to go. It's not a down funnel problem, it is an up funnel problem. And where you have to just make sure that for each role you're comfortable with the distribution of people and backgrounds in your candidate pool and go from there. And I think that is one of the reasons why that 10 person group is so effective, is it has just a lot of diversity and perspective.
turns.zh: 这些城市随处可见。去年我们提出的一个小统计数据让我深深着迷，那就是多国联合创始人团队。具体数据是，超过20%的多创始人团队至少有一位创始人来自其他国家。这让我感到震惊，互联网能让人们如此紧密相连真是太神奇了。我认为这将带来更多视角，更多的解决方案将具有本地化和全球化的特质。所有不同的观点都是宝贵的。再说回Atlas团队本身，我们在组建团队时就特别用心。团队成员以女性为主，我们在招聘时非常注重多样性，但更重要的是，我们致力于打造一个拥有不同视角的团队。你肯定经历过团队成员缺乏多样性的情形，那种情况糟糕得多。这里不需要什么高深的科学理论，我们只是严格执行这些原则。我们有机会以这种方式组建团队。对我来说，确保团队能体现我们期望的世界观非常重要。这需要用心设计，因为我职业生涯中就曾犯过错误，当我把初创公司卖给Box时，团队全是男性。在每个招聘环节，吸引不同背景的人才都变得越来越困难。人们自然而然不愿意加入这样的团队。这是我最后一次犯这种错误：候选人池必须与你期望的团队方向相契合。这不是漏斗末端的问题，而是漏斗顶端的问题。你必须确保每个职位的候选人池在背景和多样性方面都符合你的要求。正因如此，由10人组成的Atlas团队才如此高效，他们拥有丰富的多样性和不同视角。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Another skill Jeff Weinstein is incredible at that I wasn't even aware of. We're going to add them to the list and I actually saw a photo of the team and I noticed that. And so great work. Is there anything else on Atlas that you wanted to share before I get into how you actually made Atlas happen at a company like Stripe that has a billion things to do?
turns.zh: 杰夫·温斯坦（Jeff Weinstein）还有一项令人惊叹的技能，我之前甚至都不知道。我们会把这些技能加到清单里。我其实看过团队的照片，注意到了这一点。干得太棒了。在深入探讨你如何在像Stripe这样事务繁忙的公司里成功打造Atlas之前，你是否还有关于Atlas的其他想分享的信息？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: We just want to hear about what's hard for you. If you look back in your emails and if you started a company recently, you're starting a company right now, the whole world is counting on you to pick a customer, solve their problem 10 times better than their alternative, get it to them, charge for it, become economically viable and build a great business that provides great services. We are not counting on you to become experts at this silliness of administratively running your company. Imagine life without Google Docs where you'd have to hire an IT person to run your IT back end on employee three. You'd have an IT person or imagine the world without AWS for EC2 or S3 or any of these cloud services and you're racking computers yourself. (01:58:46): You're just absolutely not going to try as many things. We just see the company structure, the structure, bringing people together to be like that, and we want to automate more and more and more of it and turn it into software. So we're looking for the next things to work on. We have a couple ideas, but we expect to turn more of groups of people working together, that administration into software. And I think it's just going to unlock huge amount more people choosing to do it.
turns.zh: 我们只想听听你们遇到的难题。如果你回看之前的邮件，或者你最近刚创办一家公司，现在正在创办一家公司，全世界都在期待你能选定客户，比现有替代方案好十倍地解决他们的需求，把产品交付给他们，收费盈利，建立一个能提供优质服务的伟大企业。我们可不指望你成为行政管理公司的行家，想象一下没有Google Docs的世界，你得雇个IT人员来管理员工三号的IT后台。再想象没有AWS的EC2或S3等云服务的世界，你还得自己搭建服务器。（01:58:46）你根本没法尝试那么多东西。我们只是看到公司结构，把人们聚集在一起，形成这样的模式，我们想把越来越多的流程自动化并转化为软件。所以我们正在寻找下一个需要攻克的领域。我们有几个想法，但我们期望能把更多协同合作的团队，将行政管理工作转化为软件。我认为这将释放出更多愿意投身其中的人才。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Interesting. I'm so curious what that ends up being. If you really think about what you're doing here, if you believe that entrepreneurship and innovation and technology make the world better, you're creating such an unlock to allow more of that. And like I said, I think it's hard to imagine and think of other examples that could be as transformative and impactful as just making this process.
turns.zh: 真有意思。我特别好奇最终会是什么样子。如果你认真思考自己正在做的事情，如果你相信创业精神、创新和科技能让世界变得更美好，那你就是在为实现这一目标创造突破口。就像我说的，我很难想象还有其他能像简化这个流程一样具有变革性和影响力的例子。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: It's funny because I go back to again, I also hear from founders, entrepreneurs like, oh, I can't think of an idea. Like, ah, I need a startup idea. And yet everything in the world is broken. And I also recall my first startup early 2010, 2012 ish, I joined a friend's company. That was started at the same time that the Stripe founders started Stripe. And that is, I think about that a lot because with the same information, knowing how hard it was to accept online payments, I chose to work on something else where they didn't. They worked on making it easy in seven lines of code to accept payments online, which turned out to be really useful. (02:00:29): So I really encourage people to be very sensitive to the problems that they see and just not let any little hiccup go unnoticed. And I think Atlas is really a manifestation of that, which is, let's actually look at every single thing. You went from hobby to economically successful operation and which of any moment along the way you shouldn't have had to do. And we think those things are a fair game to play with in any topic. I think that there are many more gigantic businesses, important things to be solved sitting in plain sight. I can't see them always, but when you hear, if you sit in enough silence and you hear the same people complain about problems, you too might find something as big as online payments are hard, which was sitting right in front of all of us.
turns.zh: 这挺有趣的，因为我回想起来，创业者们也常跟我说：「我实在想不出什么点子。」或者「我需要一个创业项目。」然而这个世界到处都是亟待解决的问题。我还记得自己2010年初加入朋友公司时的创业经历——当时Stripe的创始人刚创立Stripe不久。我常回想那段经历，因为尽管我们掌握着相同的信息，却选择了不同方向。他们用七行代码就实现了在线支付功能，成果显著。（02:00:29）所以我特别鼓励人们，要对身边的问题保持敏锐，绝不能忽视任何微小的障碍。我认为Atlas就是这种理念的具体体现——我们要审视每一个细节。从爱好转向经济成功的运营过程中，哪一刻本不该如此？我们相信，任何领域都存在着亟待解决的重大难题。我并非总能发现它们，但当你静下心来倾听人们抱怨问题时，也许会发现像在线支付这样看似显而易见的难题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think it's important to note, it doesn't necessarily have to be a venture-backed, venture scale company. Right. There are many, most businesses in the world are non venture-backed, venture scale billion-dollar companies. You can build a profitable company.
turns.zh: 还要注意，这不一定非得是风投支持的风投级别公司。没错，世界上大多数非风投支持的风投级别十亿美元级公司都是盈利的。你完全可以打造一家盈利的企业。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: It's kind of funny. We've all put this badge of honor of giving away a lot of your company. People really love owning a lot of their company and being successful. So you just got to pick the right capital structure for your business.
turns.zh: 挺有意思的。我们都把把公司大量股权让出当作一种荣誉。人们其实更渴望拥有更多公司股权并取得成功。所以你只需为自己的企业选择合适的资本结构。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And again, the amount of money that has been generated of the companies that started through Atlas, you said $5 billion, basically that's the GDP of Atlas. That Atlas is,-
turns.zh: 再说了，通过Atlas平台创立的公司创造了巨额财富，你提到50亿美元，这简直就是Atlas的GDP。Atlas的营收每年都在增长，

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: And that's like revenue per year and that's growing,-
turns.zh: 而且增速惊人，

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Per year.
turns.zh: 年复一年。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. And obviously a lot of it would've happened anyway, but still it accelerated. It's probably growing faster. A lot of it probably never would've happened otherwise. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。不过显然很多事情即使没有Atlas也会发生，但Atlas确实加速了进程。可能增长得更快。很多事情可能原本根本不会发生。是啊。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: We ran a survey a little bit ago, we need to rerun this, where we just asked people would they have started their business without Atlas. And about 20% of people said they wouldn't have or wouldn't had then. And again, these things are fragile. Right. And it's not all Google employees leaving their job to the build something. It's people from every possible background, every possible role, every possible job, every possible age group who see problems and can solve it. So it's dramatically more fragile than people think.
turns.zh: 我们不久前做过一项调查，需要重新开展一下，就是询问人们如果没有Atlas会不会创业。约20%的人回答不会，或者当时不会。这些机会确实转瞬即逝。对吧？而且成功创业者不都是谷歌员工离职去创业的。来自各行各业、不同职位、不同年龄段的人，只要发现问题并能解决它，都能创造奇迹。所以成功的概率远比人们想象的低得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Well, great work, Jeff, and team Atlas and Stripe in general.
turns.zh: 杰夫，你和Atlas团队、Stripe全体成员都做得很棒。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Fun.
turns.zh: 真有意思。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let's talk about one last thing. There's so many more things I still want to talk about. Maybe we'll have a,-
turns.zh: 最后再聊一件事吧。我还有好多想聊的，或许下次再说。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: We can go quick. Yeah, we can [inaudible 02:03:08].
turns.zh: 我们可以快点结束。好的，没问题（02:03:08未听清）。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Make it 2X speed. So Atlas is basically a zero to one product. I know you didn't start initially, it was there, but you took it from, I don't know, maybe you took it from 0.5 or something to one in 100 now, and a lot of people struggle with starting things like this within larger companies. Like Stripe's a large company, right? It's like a very innovative, well run company, but it's also a large company. And clearly you made shit happen, you and your team. What kind of things have you learned? Actually, let me read a quote. Here's a quote that kind of describes you being good at this from one of your former colleagues who will go unnamed. "Jeff is really good at cutting through the BS. You hear so much about frameworks and all this complicated stuff that people talk about, NPM circles, one of the most straightforward, obvious things probably right. I get so annoyed after calls with Jeff sometimes because I know he's right about something. I banged my head against the wall for months." And so talk about just what you've done, what you've learned about getting stuff done.
turns.zh: 把速度调到两倍。Atlas基本上是从零到一的产品。我知道你们一开始不是从零开始的，它原本就存在，但你们把它从，嗯，也许从0.5左右提升到了现在的100分满分。在大公司里启动这类项目很多人都遇到了困难。比如Stripe也是个大公司，对吧？它虽然是个创新能力强、运营得当的公司，但毕竟规模不小。显然你和你的团队把事情搞定了。你们学到了哪些经验？事实上，我想引用一位前同事的话来评价你的高效。这位不愿透露姓名的前同事说：“杰夫特别善于直击核心问题。在NPM圈子里，人们总谈论各种框架和复杂技术，但杰夫能把最简单、最明显的道理说清楚。有时候和他通完电话我就很生气，因为我知道他说得对。我为此撞了好几个月的墙。”所以请分享一下你在大公司里高效完成任务的经验和心得。接下来需要做些什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Talk about what you've done, what you've learned about getting stuff done at a large company. What do you need to do?
turns.zh: 谈谈你在大公司里高效完成任务的经验和心得。接下来需要做些什么？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Not having things be your idea I think is really powerful. I just talked to 50 customers who all yelled the same thing. Here they are in varieties of quotes and forms and the rest of it, and you put some three bullet points of strategy around why it's important, it's going to help you win more market share, and the rest of it and how you can do it well. Cool. What else could we want to do? Maybe somebody has something where 51 people have the same burning thing, but the majority failure mode is we do nothing. That's the majority failure mode. So one, aligning people with deep customer stories story boarding some solution visually with a Sharpie and not a pencil, not Figma initially, not high or low fidelity. I can never remember which one is the detailed one, but Sharpie. What is the unconstrained perfect solution to this burning problem? (02:05:18): That's Pixar-style storyboard. You don't need to be a designer. You can just draw stick figures on a piece of paper or whimsical or whatever you want to do. And with those things, if you're not asking for the sun and the moon on headcount and team size to make some forward progress, who could stop you? Let's get some first version working. It was very motivating to get that single piece of paper in the mail, which was blank, to kick us off on the 83(b) election. Again, by the time this podcast airs, we'll have crossed 10,000 83(b) elections filed, and we will have done them all 100.00% on time. With the burning use case, why customers are going to need it, why we can do it cheaply, effectively, safely over a long period of time, and here's the way to get tangible, forward progress quickly against the stick figure vision, but with something in the browser or one version of it. Let's just get one thing working one time. (02:06:31): I find proof of existence to be an incredibly powerful proof, rather than proof by theory or proof by debate. It's like, "Look, we did it one time. Hey, I'm holding the piece of paper." Pretty motivating. If we just printed out the right information, we'd be done. You're like, "Okay, actually there's a lot to do other than just that," but it really pushed us forward. Cutting through a little bit of the red tape is about momentum and making each step not such a big deal and asking for less permission. Then of course, once you have a little bit of that under your belt, you're going to naturally be trusted with taking more of those kinds of bets. (02:07:24): Paired with some of the things we talked about earlier of everyone's looking at the same place about the metrics, everyone can watch the success. We don't need to do big, internal updates with long-winded PowerPoint presentations and scrambles the night before. You can just go to the metrics page and see how we're doing. That brings so much trust to the group that people start going from, "Why do we have this Atlas thing that doesn't really produce so much money. It's charging companies when they don't have money. We're a big payments business. How do you even compare these things?" To "Wow, look at the progress that they're making against the mission, and look at its impact on the curves." And you start to root for it more. (02:08:16): I think that's how we got it there. I will say one other thing, which is that making something economically viable is extremely important. I am probably the fourth person to run Atlas, and it's quite a pantheon of people prior to me, including the founder of Mozi, which is a compliance startup, Watershed, which is this amazing climate reporting tool, also led Atlas, Patrick McKenzie, patio11, for many folks who [inaudible 02:08:46]
turns.zh:
我认为不让事情成为你的主意，这真的很重要。我刚刚和50位客户交流，他们都说了同样的话。以下是他们的各种观点和建议，你可以用三个要点来概括策略的核心：为什么这很重要？如何赢得更多市场份额？以及如何做好这件事。太棒了。我们还能做些什么？也许有人会发现51个人都有同样迫切的需求，但大多数人的失败模式是无所作为。这才是多数人的失败模式。首先，要让团队与客户深度共鸣，用记号笔而非Figma等工具直观地勾勒解决方案框架。（02:05:18）：这就是皮克斯式的故事板。你不需要是设计师，只要在纸上画些简笔人物或随心所欲的图形就行。只要不要求过高的团队规模或头衔就能取得进展，谁能阻止你呢？先推出初版产品。把那张空白纸邮寄出去就能启动83(b)选举流程，这真的很激励人。等播客播出时，我们已经提交了超过1万份83(b)选举申请，且全部100%按时完成。有了这个紧迫的用例——客户为何需要它？我们为何能低成本、高效、安全地长期提供服务？以下是如何快速通过简笔视觉验证取得切实进展的方法——先在浏览器中实现一个版本。只要成功一次就够了。（02:06:31）：我发现存在性验证比理论证明或辩论证明更有力。比如：“看，我们成功了一次。嘿，我手里就拿着这张纸。”这太有激励力了。如果我们只打印出正确的信息，就大功告成了。但这其实推动了我们前进。削减一些繁琐程序关键在于保持动力，降低每一步的难度，并减少审批流程。当然，一旦你积累了一些经验，人们自然会信任你去承担更多这类风险。（02:07:24）：再结合我们之前提到的所有内容——所有人都在关注同样的指标，每个人都能看到成功进展。我们无需通过冗长的PowerPoint演示和前夜的紧急准备来进行内部更新。你只需访问指标页面就能看到我们的进展。这为团队带来了极大的信任，从“为什么我们要做Atlas这个根本不怎么赚钱的项目？它向没钱的公司收费，我们可是大型支付业务，根本没法比较这些东西。”转变为“哇，看看他们在实现使命方面取得的进展，以及对数据曲线的影响。”然后你会更加支持他们。（02:08:16）：我觉得这就是我们成功的秘诀。我还要说一点，让产品在经济上可行非常重要。我可能是Atlas的第四任负责人，之前有不少大牛前辈，包括合规初创公司Mozi的创始人、出色的气候报告工具Watershed的创始人，以及Atlas的前任负责人Patrick。
麦肯齐（McKenzie）、帕蒂奥11（patio11），对许多人来说，[02:08:46未录音]

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, what an alumni group, this collection.
turns.zh: 哇，这群校友真是了不起，这份合集太棒了。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: We owe ourselves a dinner. We owe ourselves a dinner. Quite a group. And now we have a new person. I technically no longer lead Atlas, so we've hired up a whole team, which is really exciting. And Hayley Halvarsson, who's joined us about a year or two ago, she leads Atlas now and you can find her on Twitter. She's fantastic. We swap jobs over a course of a year, just one month at a time, the roles. And so she worked for me, then I worked for her, and she's gone off to hire some amazing people to run Atlas. So it's really quite a privilege to have these people lead it over time. (02:09:22): But it was really important for us to communicate why we were going to run this in an economically viable way, and I think that applies to all products and all businesses. It's like, "Look, if you're a customer acquisition-style product, showcase why this is the best customer acquisition for the dollar for the company. If you are a margin-generating, moat-creating, ecosystem-growing portion of the business, then your metrics have to show it." So you can't just have half the story of just the product quality and the tweets. You have to have the economics. Who else is going to put this much energy into this style of product and that gives us confidence that we should invest it in the long term? Because alternatives can come and go, and I super encourage there to be more Atlas alternatives. That'd be great for founders, but I think over the long term, it'll be difficult to do so because of the business model.
turns.zh: 我们该请自己吃顿饭。请自己吃顿饭。这真是个很棒的团队。现在我们又迎来了一位新成员。严格来说，我已经不再负责Atlas项目了，所以我们组建了一整个团队，这真的很令人兴奋。大约一两年前加入我们的海莉·哈尔瓦森，现在负责Atlas项目，你们可以在推特上找到她。她非常出色。我们每年都会轮换工作岗位，每次只换一个月。先是我为她工作，然后她为我工作，现在她已经招募了很棒的人来运营Atlas项目。能让这些人才逐渐接手管理工作，真是莫大的荣幸。（02:09:22）但对我们来说，关键是要向大家解释为什么我们要以经济可行的方式运营这个项目，我认为这适用于所有产品和业务。比如，“看，如果你是一款客户获取类产品，就要展示为什么这是公司花钱最值的客户获取方式。如果你是一款能创造利润护城河、推动生态系统发展的业务板块，那么你的数据就必须能体现这一点。”不能只讲产品质量和推特互动的一面，还得有经济数据。谁会投入如此多精力打造这种类型的产品？这让我们有信心长期投入资源。因为替代品来来去去，我非常鼓励出现更多Atlas的替代品，这对创业者来说是好事，但从长远看，这很难实现，因为商业模式的限制。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There actually was an alternative at one point, AngelList, and then they're like, "No, Stripe is killing it. Let's just send everyone to Atlas."
turns.zh: 实际上曾经有过一个替代品，叫AngelList，但他们后来就说：“不行，Stripe太强了。我们还是把所有人都引流到Atlas吧。”

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I had worked on Stripe payments for a while, and I had just started on Atlas, and I think that same month AngelList announced that they were doing incorporation and banking and cap table all together, which was exactly what I wanted to do. I was like, "Oh shoot, did I sign up for the wrong thing? AngelList is such a smart group of people, so customer-oriented, great brand, I love many of the people that work there, they work with some of the best legal minds, and they have the RUV setup. There's so much awesomeness here." I was like, " Should we really compete? What should we do here?" And we thought about it more and more like, "Look, in the very long term, this company-starting process is going to become a efficiency cost problem, and there's so much long tail complexity with dealing with multiple financial institutions, multiple government processes, all of this legal complexity, and it's difficult to charge a lot of money for it because it's hard to charge people money when they haven't even started the business yet." (02:11:36): We looked at it and said, "Look, we're going to keep this long-term, compounding approach because we think that this is where it's going to go." And it was a zero interest rate environment at the time. AngelList built a phenomenal product. I looked at it with nothing but admiration and happiness, but it also smarted and hurt. We kept building, kept building, kept building, and I got a phone call one night, on my wife's birthday before we sat down for dinner, and it was Dan at AngelList, I hope he'd be comfortable telling the story, who I love. Incredible product mind and he led product over AngelList for startups. He said, "We're going to get out of incorporation. This is not going to be our focus going forward. Do you want the business?" (02:12:28): That was like a year and a half after they had really gone out, or maybe two years after they'd gone out, or something like this. I was like, "Wow." We had kept such an open relationship with them. We had paired with them on legal constructs. We had discussed 83(b) election openly. A lot of people were like, "I can't believe you're talking to the competitor." Look, we all share the same mission here. Yes, we're competing, but are we really all better off from treating each other at arm's distance? We had a shared Slack channel. We discussed when the Delaware was slow on incorporation. One time is because they were playing softball and they had an afternoon off. That's a real story, and we've discussed it. AngelList was incredible in how they evaluated it. We're evaluating different partners, but because of our working relationship and the quality of your product, and they saw we were going with 83(b) election and the intensity of that, they just put up a webpage that said to get started with AngelList, if you need a company, go right over to Atlas. (02:13:36): That was a really amazing moment because I respected them so much and I looked up to them so much that they would mutually beneficially choose to do that. And everybody was excited and happy, and customers are happy, and it's been an incredible relationship since, in which you can start on AngelList, go through Atlas, and then all of your information is automatically populated into AngelList automatically. We've since rolled that out with several other partners, Mercury, Carta, others, but AngelList really led the way there, and we maintain a great relationship with the team. It took a while, but it really reproved to me that they're not competitors. It's alternatives, and if you care about your customer, you care about their alternatives, and if you care about the mission, you need to all work together. Look, there's some friendly competition, of course. We all want to win, but in the long term, I think all parties are significantly better off.
turns.zh:
我曾在Stripe支付领域工作了一段时间，刚开始着手Atlas项目。同月时，AngelList宣布将把公司注册、银行开户和股权结构等全套服务整合在一起——这正是我当时想做的事情。我当时想：“天哪，我是不是报名错了？AngelList团队如此聪明，客户至上，品牌出色，我喜欢那里的许多员工，他们与顶尖法律团队合作，还有RUV（注册后验证）系统。这里简直太棒了。” 但我又疑惑：“我们真的要竞争吗？该怎么办？”  

我们反复思考后认为：“从长远来看，这个创业流程将成为效率成本问题。而处理多家金融机构、政府程序及复杂法律事务的后续影响又会带来长尾效应。况且新创企业尚未启动时很难收取高额服务费。” （02:11:36）  

我们决定坚持长期复合式发展策略：“我们坚信这是行业趋势。” 当时正值零利率环境。AngelList打造了卓越产品。我满怀敬意与喜悦审视它，但这种审视也带来刺痛。我们持续开发，直到某晚——在我妻子生日前夕、晚餐前接到电话——是Dan打来的。他曾领导AngelList的初创企业产品线，我很欣赏他。  

Dan说：“我们将退出公司注册服务。这不再是我们的核心业务。你们想要这项业务吗？” （02:12:28）  

这距离他们真正退出市场已有一年半，或许两年之久。我惊讶道：“哇！” 我们与他们保持开放合作关系，共同探讨法律架构，公开讨论83(b)选举条款。许多人惊讶：“难以置信你们和竞争对手合作！” 但我们秉持共同使命。是的，我们在竞争，但保持距离是否真能双赢？我们共享Slack频道，讨论特拉华州注册延迟问题。有次是因为他们打棒球，下午休息日延迟了。这些真实故事至今仍被提及。  

AngelList对我们的评估极为专业。我们评估不同合作伙伴，但鉴于合作关系和产品质量，以及我们坚持83(b)选举的决心，他们直接上线网页，告知用户需用Atlas注册公司。  

（02:13:36）  

这真是个惊喜时刻。我对他们充满敬意，他们选择互利合作。客户满意度极高，此后关系更加紧密。用户可在AngelList注册，再转入Atlas，所有信息自动同步。我们已与Mercury、Carta等多家合作伙伴复制了这种模式，但AngelList始终是先锋。我们保持着良好的合作关系。这段经历让我确信，他们不是竞争对手，而是替代方案。只要你真心为客户着想，合作才能水到渠成。
客户，你们关心他们的替代方案，而如果你们关心这个使命，就需要携手合作。当然，友好竞争是存在的。我们都想赢，但从长远来看，我认为各方都会受益匪浅。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, that is an awesome story. I don't know if you've shared that anywhere else. There's so many lessons there that I could spin off on and... Not worrying about competition, staying heads down, just solving customer problems, staying close to your competition, not being afraid to talk to them, sharing advice with each other, just building the best possible product. I don't know, there's a ton there that's super interesting.
turns.zh: 哇，这真是个超棒的故事。我不知道你是否在其他地方分享过这个故事。里面有很多值得深思的启示，比如……不必担忧竞争，埋头苦干，专注解决客户问题，与竞争对手保持密切沟通，勇于交流经验，打造最优质的产品。说实话，其中有很多观点都非常有趣。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I couldn't really draw it up any better, and I think the world is better off with more specialization, and it's a pain in the butt to do these incorporations. I think you want more specialization and more partnership, and I think a lot of companies are starting to do that now.
turns.zh: 我实在想不出比这更好的总结了。我认为世界需要更多专业化分工，但这些公司合并过程实在太耗费精力了。我认为大家应该追求专业化分工和深度合作，现在很多公司都开始朝这个方向发展了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Let me go back to the lessons you shared on how to build something new at a big company, then we can wrap up. I took a bunch of notes here, and these are awesome and they actually resonate a lot with Mihika, who came on the podcast, who's at Figma, been the person building a lot of zero-to-one stuff. So it's nice that there's these trends that are coming up again and again. (02:15:32): One tip is storyboard the ideal. With a Sharpie, draw out, "Here's this exciting vision of what this could be if we were to pull it off without constraints." Unconstrained, powerful vision. Two is solve a burning use case. Make it clear this is a huge problem for a lot of people. There's probably stories you share there. Show tangible forward progress like, "Look at this, we made this progress, we made this progress. Sent ourselves a piece of blank paper. Look at this, it's a huge milestone." And have momentum, and Mihika talked about this. Keep the fire alive. Keep the fire alive, show momentum. We're making progress. This metrics moving up into the right. Then there's a milestone... Felt like you had an early milestone of like, "Look, we made progress," and then also, have the business case, basically. "Look how much we could make and look what this could be if we were to succeed." Anything you'd add there? Anything you'd correct?
turns.zh: 接下来我想回归你分享的在大公司创新创业的经验，然后结束这次讨论。我在这边做了不少笔记，这些内容非常棒，也和我们请到的Figma公司的Mihika产生了强烈共鸣。她在节目中分享的很多零到一的创新案例都和我们今天讨论的主题不谋而合。很高兴看到这些创新趋势不断涌现。（02:15:32）第一条建议是构想理想蓝图。用记号笔勾勒出“如果没有任何限制，我们能把这个愿景变为现实”的激动人心的蓝图。这种不受约束的宏大愿景非常重要。第二条是解决痛点。要让大家清楚这个问题对很多人来说都是巨大的挑战。你可能需要分享相关案例。展示切实的进展，比如“看看我们取得了这些成果，我们发送了一张空白纸张。再看看这个，这是一个重要的里程碑。”保持势头很重要，Mihika也提到过这一点。要让激情持续燃烧，不断展示进展，让大家看到数据在向好的方向发展，然后设定一个重要的里程碑……比如“看，我们取得了初步进展”，同时也要阐明商业价值，“看看我们能赚多少钱，如果成功了会带来怎样的机遇。”你有什么补充或修正吗？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Bringing the earliest customers into the room with your team as soon as humanly possible. We would just invite a founder to the team meeting. We would pipe all their feedback into a Slack channel automatically. We have all the NPS scores going to a channel, and anytime it's not a 10 for 10, we follow up directly. Constant engagement with a customer creates the momentum where it doesn't need to be the product person or some other leader saying, "We need to do this. Follow me." It's, "Oh my gosh, the world needs this. Let's figure out how to do it even faster." (02:17:06): And a tip that the team has tried, and this is well since I've been involved day-to-day, is literally inviting customers in to design the product, which I'd actually never heard of. "Hey, we're thinking about what happens after incorporation now and what can we do to help founders after they've set up their company? What would be magical there?" We just invite founders in, into a Whimsical, a piece of software I love. It's a really easy learning curve to create visual diagrams. And rather than doing a UXR about it, we just say, "What would you hope this dashboard would have?" And they'd grab a thing, and they start typing, and they start drawing what they want their dashboard to be. Why were we guessing beforehand? I now scratch my head. I'm several years into a decade-plus building things and I was like, "I doing this by myself. Why didn't I just assign it to the people who are going to use it in the first place?" (02:18:01): Now look, that doesn't always work because not all of your customers are going to be product designers at heart, but more of them than you think, and I think it's giving your customers write access, and not just read access, to your company is incredibly powerful. I think I had not quite seen it so directly where you just actually designed what they want, but I saw a diagram of something we're working on right now. I was like, "Wow, we haven't even had design look at it." They're like, "No, actually the customer drew it." Great. Why were we guessing?
turns.zh: 尽可能快地让最早的客户与你的团队同处一室。我们会直接邀请创始人参加团队会议，并自动将他们的所有反馈导入Slack频道。我们把所有NPS评分都放进一个频道，每当评分低于10分时，我们都会立即跟进。与客户持续互动能形成一种势头——无需产品经理或其他领导者说：“我们需要这样做，跟我来。”而是：“天哪，这个世界需要这个功能。让我们想办法更快实现它。”（02:17:06）：团队尝试过的一个方法（自从我参与日常工作以来）就是邀请客户参与产品设计。这是我从未听说过的做法。“嘿，我们现在在思考公司注册后会发生什么，能做些什么帮助创始人？怎样才能更完美？”我们邀请创始人进入Whimsical（一款我很喜欢的软件），创建视觉图表的学习曲线很简单。我们没有做用户体验研究，而是直接问：“你希望这个仪表板有什么功能？”他们拿起工具开始输入和绘制自己理想中的仪表板。我们之前为什么要猜测？现在回想起来真是愚蠢至极。我有十多年产品开发经验，却总以为自己能独自完成这些工作。为什么不直接把任务交给最先使用它的人呢？（02:18:01）：当然，这方法并非万能，因为并非所有客户都是天生产品设计师，但远比你想象的多。我认为赋予客户对公司的写入权限（而非仅限读取权限）非常强大。虽然我之前没见过客户直接设计产品，但我现在看到了我们正在开发的某个产品的示意图。我惊叹道：“哇，我们甚至还没让设计团队看过这个。”他们回答：“不，客户自己画的。” 太棒了。我们之前为什么要猜测呢？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you have an unfair advantage where your customers are founders and oftentimes have product skills and design skills, but I love that [inaudible 02:18:43].
turns.zh: 你确实有得天独厚的优势——你的客户本身就是创始人，往往具备产品和设计技能，但我真的很欣赏你提到的这种方法[02:18:43]。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: It's true, but I will really push, because you don't need a hundred of them and you'll find somebody somewhere who knows. You just got to sit in a little more silence. They'll raise their hand.
turns.zh: 确实如此，但我会继续努力推广，因为你不需要一百个客户，只要在某个地方能找到懂行的人就行。你只需要多花点时间倾听。他们会主动发声的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a quote you shared somewhere that relates to what you just said that your dad once said, "You can screw up a sentence if it begins with 'The customer.'"
turns.zh: 你之前分享过一句引语，关于你父亲曾说过：“如果一句话以‘客户’开头，你很可能要把它搞砸了。”

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: That's true. Yeah, my dad runs an IT business in Baltimore to help other businesses with their computer systems. Growing up, I would literally, physically clean the keyboards of his employees and dust the mice. But yeah, he's very, very customer-oriented, where I get a lot of it from, and my mom's a painter, so I think there's some combination of talents or interests there. He would take it one step further, and he sometimes physically bring a chair over in a meeting and say, "The customer is sitting here," and you'd have to pretend. Then he would fake talk to the invisible customer. "Based on what you've seen today at the meeting..." I saw him do this one time. "Based on what you've seen today at the meeting, are you more likely to pay your bill or less likely to pay your bill based on what you witnessed?" (02:19:55): That's a little intense on the pantomime, but I think the point gets across that... Again, because it's so natural to think internal, if you begin the sentence physically with "The customer" then start your sentence, you just have a much better shot at it.
turns.zh: 确实如此。是啊，我父亲在巴尔的摩经营一家IT公司，帮助其他企业维护计算机系统。小时候，我真的会亲手清理员工的键盘，擦拭鼠标。但说真的，他对客户服务非常用心，这一点我深受影响。我母亲是一位画家，所以我觉得这两种才能或兴趣在某种程度上互补。他甚至更进一步，有时在会议上亲自搬来椅子说：“客户就坐在这里。”然后你得假装与这位看不见的客户交流。“根据你今天在会议上看到的情况……”（02:19:55）：这种假装动作确实有点夸张，但我想意思已经传达清楚了……再说了，因为我们习惯从内部视角思考，如果你用“客户”来开头，接着再展开句子，这样成功的概率会大得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an amazing story. Very a study group-ish, like an early prototype. Jeff, we've covered so much ground. I have two hours more worth of questions, but we need to-
turns.zh: 这真是个精彩的故事。很像学习小组的氛围，简直是早期原型。杰夫，我们已经讨论了这么多内容。我还有两个小时的问题要问，但我们得——

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Let's lock.
turns.zh: 结束了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: We need to cut it off, I think. Is there anything else you wanted to share or leave listeners with before we get to a very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 我想我们得结束了。在进入激动人心的闪电问答环节之前，你还有什么想和听众分享或留给他们的吗？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Really excited about whatever you're building out there, thinking of building. My email address is incredibly easy to find. My Twitter handle is incredibly easy to find. Do not hesitate to send me cold emails. My love language is Loom videos of bugs, but feel free to send anything you have off the top of your head. I respond to good cold emails. Don't hesitate.
turns.zh: 我对你们正在开发或考虑开发的项目非常兴奋。我的邮箱地址很容易找到，Twitter账号也很容易找到。别犹豫，随时给我发邮件。我最喜欢看Loom上的漏洞视频，但你有什么想法随时分享。我会回复优质的冷邮件，别犹豫。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What's the email, real quick, for people?
turns.zh: 邮箱地址是什么？快告诉大家！

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: If finding my email address is your issue? It can't possibly be, but it is my first initial and last name at basically everything in the world, though my handle on Twitter is jeff_weinstein, but gosh, if you can't find my email address then you got a bigger problem.
turns.zh: 如果找不到我的邮箱地址？这应该不可能，但我的名字首字母和姓氏在世界上几乎所有地方都适用，不过Twitter账号是jeff_weinstein。不过天哪，如果你连邮箱都找不到，那你就麻烦大了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, we'll link to it in the show notes, as well. With that, we've reached our very exciting lightning round. Are you ready? Here we go. What are two or three books you've recommended most to other people?
turns.zh: 好的，我们也会在节目笔记中附上链接。接下来是激动人心的闪电问答环节。准备好了吗？开始吧。你向别人推荐最多的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I know a lot of people on this podcast recommend high-output management, but it should be swap the Bible out for it at all the hotels in the world, in the little drawer. Put it everywhere. You can't go wrong, though. It is an incredible clarity of how to spend your time as a leader, a manager of other people, a very high bar for how evaluating your work as the sum everyone around you. That was very clarifying to me that it's not an individual effort, it is the sum of everything I'm involved in is how to measure it. So that's definitely up there. A nice pair to that book, as a amuse-bouche afterwards, is Orbiting the Giant Hairball: A Corporate Fool's Guide to Surviving with Grace, I think, is the full exact title by Gordon MacKenzie, which is the story of a illustrator at Hallmark, the greeting card company, and it turns out to be a, again, bureaucratic, slow-moving organization that, over time, added rules and policies and rules and policies and quelled creativity and innovation, which is surprising at a greeting card company, but it existed. So this is his incredibly well-drawn book, as you'd imagine, with beautiful illustrations about how he orbited the hairball of the organization to inspire others, keep himself engaged, and to bring creativity and excitement and trying to pull people off the hairball as he orbited it. So I think it's a fun afternoon read with beautiful illustrations about how to stay sane at big companies and where to be a little goofy and take the advantage and gravity of the hairball, but not be succumbed by it and to be able to orbit it. (02:23:22): Those two are really fun. I will say one other one I like... Because we haven't talked about strategy here, there's been more getting stuff done and some other tactical things, but 7 Powers, and I know you had the author recently on, which was awesome. I won't explain the book, you just watch the podcast of it, but it walks through many of the business powers and moats a company can have. I ran into the author...
turns.zh:
我知道这个播客里很多人推荐《高效能管理》，但我觉得应该把《圣经》换成这本书，放在全球所有酒店的小抽屉里。随处可见。但这本书确实很棒。它清晰地阐释了作为领导者、管理者如何分配时间，为评估工作成果设定极高标准。对我来说，最深刻的启发是成功不是个人的努力，而是你所参与的所有事务的总和。这让我意识到，成功绝非个人之功，而是一个系统性工程。

作为补充读物，我推荐戈登·麦肯齐的《绕过巨型发胶球：在企业中优雅生存的指南》。这本书讲述了贺卡公司Hallmark一位插画师的故事。Hallmark本质上是一个官僚化、运转迟缓的组织，层层叠叠的规章制度扼杀了创造力与创新精神。即便在贺卡公司这样的行业，这一现象也令人震惊。但麦肯齐以生动的插画和幽默的笔触，描绘了自己如何在组织的迷宫中破局，激发团队活力，释放创造力与激情，并帮助他人摆脱困境。这是一本充满智慧的读物，既有深刻的管理洞察，又不失趣味性。

（02:23:22）：这两本书都非常有趣。我还想推荐另一本——《7种力量》。我们在播客里没怎么谈战略，更多是谈执行和战术，但这本书很棒，前不久我们邀请了作者上节目，非常精彩。我就不多解释书的内容了，大家可以去看播客，但书中系统梳理了企业可以拥有的多种商业力量和护城河。我曾遇到过作者……

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Hamilton Helmer.
turns.zh: 汉密尔顿·赫尔默。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Hamilton Helmer, yes, thank you.
turns.zh: 汉密尔顿·赫尔默，是的，谢谢。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What a cool name.
turns.zh: 真是个酷名字。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Very cool name. Alliterative. At the Box lunchroom one time, where I worked at Box, they acquired one of our companies, and I was like, "Any luck finding the eighth power?" He was like, "I'm looking, I'm looking," as he ran off with his sandwich. One other funny, somewhat embarrassing moment about that book is when I was applying to work at Stripe, I was in some email conversation with our CEO, Patrick Collison, who is quite well-read and enjoys books, and I was trying to showcase, " I like books a little bit," though not at any level of him. And I had mentioned I just finished reading 7 Powers, and I recommended it to him, but it joke's on me because he's quoted in the foreword that I had skipped. So he was very kind to let me know that he had read it and he is quoted in it, so I was like, "Oh shoot, maybe I won't get the job." But I got through that part, at least. So those books have spoken to me. Do you have a favorite power, by the way, Lenny? Do you have a favorite power?
turns.zh: 非常酷的名字。押韵。在Box的午餐室，有一次他们收购了我们的一家公司，我问：“找到第八种力量了吗？”他说：“我在找，在找。”然后就跑去吃三明治了。关于那本书还有个有趣又尴尬的小插曲，我申请Stripe工作时，和他们的CEO帕特里克·科利森聊天，发现他博览群书，尤其喜欢书籍。我想展示自己对书籍的喜爱，尽管远不及他。当时我刚读完《7种力量》，还向他推荐了，结果玩了个文字游戏——他在前言中被引用了，而我恰好跳过了那段。幸好他很友善地告诉我他读过这本书，还被引用了，不然我可能就没机会了。但至少我克服了这个障碍。这两本书真的触动了我。顺便问一句，莱尼，你最喜欢的力量是什么？你最喜欢的力量是什么？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: His favorite power is counter-positioning. I also like that power a lot because I think it's the one you can that really changes everything about how you build your company, so that's the one that always stands out to me. How about you?
turns.zh: 他最喜欢的力量是反向定位。我也很喜欢这个力量，因为我认为它能彻底改变你构建公司的思路，所以它一直让我印象深刻。你呢？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I like counter-positioning also, and Atlas with going cheap and that audience is counter-positioning, but I really enjoy process, the process power, because it is very difficult to, as an organization, get good at anything, and if you could do that over a long period of time in a sustainable way, you have a power.
turns.zh: 我也喜欢反向定位，比如Atlas采取低价策略，这种反向定位策略很棒。但我真正热衷的是流程力量——流程化思维。一个组织要想在某个领域精通并非易事，而若能长期、可持续地做到这一点，那就是一种真正的核心竞争力。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This is the nerdiest chat I've ever had. Which is your favorite 7th Power? I love it. But on that power, I asked him about it. He makes a really strong point there, that rarely is it actually a power for people. They think the way we execute is going to be our advantage and rarely is it actually a power. Usually people can copy it, but when you nail it...
turns.zh: 这真是我参与过的最烧脑的聊天了。你们最喜欢的第七大竞争力是什么？我超爱这个概念。但关于这项竞争力，我向他提问时，他提出了一个深刻见解：人们往往误以为执行方式会成为我们的竞争优势，但实际上这很少能真正转化为竞争力。因为竞争对手通常能模仿，但若我们能做到极致——

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: That's even better, because then if your competition thinks they have it-
turns.zh: 那就更好了。因为如果竞争对手认为自己已经掌握了这种优势——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 没错，就是这样。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: They won't invest than the other one. So I like it even more, for that reason.
turns.zh: 他们就不会投入比对手更多的资源了。所以正因如此，我更欣赏它。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love it. But I was going to say with Patrick Collison being quoted in the book, not only was he wrote part of the forward or was quoted, he basically credited 7 Powers of helping build Stripe. No big deal.
turns.zh: 我超爱这个概念。但我本来想说，在书中引用Patrick Collison的例子时，他不仅写了序言或被引用，更重要的是，他把《七种竞争力》视为帮助Stripe发展的重要因素。这没什么大不了的。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Totally.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This lightning around is going great. This is a very microcosm of our whole chat so far. Second question, do you have a favorite recent movie or TV show?
turns.zh: 这次闪电对话进行得非常顺利。这完全是我们迄今为止整个聊天的缩影。第二个问题，近期你最喜欢的电影或电视剧是什么？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: How To with John Wilson. It's on HBO. For those who haven't seen it, not really giving away anything because it's just wild when you watch it. You can't give it away. This videographer has found footage where he's just walking through Manhattan, and other parts of the country, but mostly New York, with a camera for 10 years, just filming intensely weird things. And if you've spent any time in New York, there's plenty to film. Then has put together this narrative afterwards about certain topics like how to make risotto or how to take out the trash or how to... (02:26:53): It's a way of seeing life through the eyes of these vignettes, diving down and really understanding people, and he does it through this incredibly dry humor of stitching together this video footage to tell a different narrative. And I think some of it is that we used to live in New York, and I love living in California, but I miss that frequency of strangeness, and you can see that through that TV show. Fantastic. (02:27:26): Movie? I recently watched The Quiet Girl, which is a film about a young Irish girl who is from a dysfunctional home and has this opportunity to live with a family friend who have more opportunity for her, more empathetic to her, and it showcases, again, how fragile things are. It's a very intense film, but there's something beautiful in how much opportunity was in front of this young girl. It is a tearjerker, but a great one.
turns.zh: 《How To with John Wilson》。这部剧在HBO播出。没看过的人，我不剧透太多，因为看的时候真的很震惊，根本无法用语言形容。这位摄影师收集了10年来在曼哈顿和美国其他地方（尤其是纽约）拍摄的各种奇特素材，然后围绕特定主题（比如如何做意大利调味饭、如何倒垃圾、如何……）编织叙事故事。（02:26:53）：这部剧通过这些小片段，让我们以独特视角观察生活，深入理解人性。他用极其冷幽默的剪辑手法，将这些素材拼凑成不同的叙事故事。我想正是因为我们曾在纽约生活过，又热爱加州生活，才会深切怀念那种奇特感的频率，而这部剧能完美呈现这种情感。太棒了。（02:27:26）：电影方面？我最近看了《安静的女孩》，这部电影讲述了一个爱尔兰女孩出身于破碎家庭，获得机会与更富有同情心的亲友生活在一起的故事。它再次展现了事物易碎的本质。这部电影非常震撼，但能从中看到这个女孩本可拥有的巨大机会。确实催人泪下，但却很棒。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have a favorite product you have recently discovered that you love?
turns.zh: 你最近有没有发现什么超爱的新产品？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I love my computer. I'm fast at my computer. Being fast at my computer helps me just go from intention to just out in the world. I've fallen back in love with Raycast, which is an automation tool for those who have watched the journey of Spotlight and Quicksilver and Alfred and all these automator services. Raycast seems to have cracked the nut on automation, nerd complexity, but also UI ease and some nice touches and loads quickly, does the basics. It's fully programmable, extensible, just a huge fan of Raycast. And then I think for product people, if you don't have CleanShot installed for screenshots, you're behind the curve. Being able to take a screenshot and blur particular things or point at stuff or have arrows and lines and have that be second nature, fast, instantaneous is so useful to be able to communicate what you're seeing. When I get a new laptop, it's Raycast first and CleanShot second.
turns.zh: 我超爱我的电脑。我用电脑速度很快。用电脑能让我迅速将想法转化为现实。最近我又重新爱上了Raycast这款自动化工具——对于那些见证过Spotlight、Quicksilver、Alfred等自动化服务发展历程的人来说，Raycast无疑是破解自动化难题的利器。它完美平衡了极客级别的复杂性与界面易用性，加载迅速，基础功能齐全。它完全可编程、可扩展，我简直是Raycast的狂热粉丝。还有，如果你还没安装CleanShot这款截图工具，那可就落伍了。用它能快速截图并模糊特定区域、标注重点、添加箭头线条，这些操作就像第二天性一样自然高效，能有效传达信息。当我换新笔记本时，首选Raycast，其次才是CleanShot。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, I am going to download CleanShot immediately.
turns.zh: 哇，我要马上下载CleanShot。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Yes, it's extremely-
turns.zh: 是啊，它太棒了——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I've not heard of it. I've been using Skitch as my blurrings.
turns.zh: 我没听说过这个工具，一直用Skitch来模糊图片。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: As much as I appreciate the Skitch folks, CleanShot is an incredible piece of software.
turns.zh: 尽管我很欣赏Skitch团队，但CleanShot确实是款超赞的软件。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I'm going to do that. All right, two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to, share with friends or family, find useful in work or in life?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我现在就去试试。好的，最后两个问题。你有没有特别喜欢的座右铭，经常挂在嘴边、分享给朋友或家人，或者在工作和生活中觉得很有用？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I don't even realize I say "Go Go Go" a lot, but I do. I actually say it and write it so people I hear that they'll later say, "Go Go Go" back to me. I'm like, "Huh? Don't I say that sometimes?" "Yes, you say it a lot." So apparently, "Go Go Go" is one of them. I also-
turns.zh: 我甚至没意识到自己常说"冲冲冲"，但确实经常说。每次有人听到我说这句话，后来又回敬我时，我都特别惊讶："什么？我不是常说吗？" "是啊，你老是说啊。" 看来"冲冲冲"确实是我的口头禅之一。我还——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that.
turns.zh: 我超爱这句话。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Say, "Let's make some mistakes," when we're brainstorming something or sitting at a sushi restaurant and talk sushi guy or gal, to showcase, "Let's be creative. Do whatever you want. No pretense. I'm not evaluating anything. Let's make some mistakes." It's just a weird thing.
turns.zh: 比如，我们头脑风暴新项目时，或者坐在寿司店跟寿司师傅聊天时，就会说："别太在意细节。大胆发挥吧。没关系的，我不评判。咱们就尽情犯错吧。" 这听起来有点怪。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: They're so good. I'm going to use that for my podcast guests. "Let's just make some mistakes. Don't worry about it."
turns.zh: 它们太棒了。我要在播客中用给嘉宾听："咱们就随便试试，别太在意结果。"

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: At that point, everyone's like, "What? Okay, fine. Sure. Cool."
turns.zh: 这时候大家都会说："什么？好吧，不介意，随便试试。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like the combo of those two, "Go go go, let's just make some mistakes while we're going."
turns.zh: 我喜欢这两句话的组合："冲冲冲，咱们边做边试错。"

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: You have to use it in certain circumstances and not for the five nines of reliability on our API, but it does have its place.
turns.zh: 有些情况下你得用它，但别指望它能达到API的五个9级可靠性标准，不过它确实有其价值。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Final question. You worked with Patrick Collison and John Collison for many years. I'm curious what the most useful feedback or advice you have heard from them or learned from them?
turns.zh: 最后一个问题。你和Patrick Collison、John Collison共事多年。我很好奇你从他们那里得到的最有用的反馈或建议是什么？

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: On my first month working here, which I guess is six, seven years ago now, they had put me in charge of our payments infrastructure services. That's all the backend systems that communicate with the financial system and all the internal APIs where we build the external APIs and products on top of, so quite a lot of stuff. I knew nothing about finance. I knew nothing about the scale that we're talking about. They entrusted me, somewhat insanely, with that responsibility. On the first month we had our quarterly business review where... The normal quarterly process, and I was like, "Okay, cool. I'll do the next one. I'll write the next one." I've been here one month. They're like, "No, you write it. It'll be even better that you write it." It's like, oh my God. It's forcing me to have to, in the fourth week, have that catalyst to understand the whole business and with the permission, because I was going to have to write this doc about how we're doing. The company had been in existence for seven years before I got here. It was already at some reasonable scale. (02:31:54): It was an intense operation, and I remember writing the first draft and sending it to him because it was... I didn't want to send... He had pushed me to do it a bit, and I figured I'd give him an early draft and he wrote back, "This doesn't sound like you yet." The willingness to entrust a new person to provide their own perspective and bring it into a very formalized document like that was an impressive... That really spoke to me, and I rewrote it completely, and I made it sound like me, and I've tried to make things sound like me since. (02:32:29): John's is more of a gut punch, I'll say. I reported to John, the co-founder. Maybe nine months into reporting to him, I would run around with a clipboard. I was a little bit manic of getting a lot done. A lot going on at Stripe at the time. We'd have a one-hour one-on-one, I'd be listing all of the things that we had accomplished and the problems we have and where we need escalation help and where we're stuck and all this that and the other. Lots of stuff. I had checklists and physical paper, flipping it over a little bit frantically. And he said, "You are one of the best people I've ever worked with at solving problems three through 100, but I need you stuck on problems one and two." (02:33:22): Oh man, that hurt. I was like, "Oh, shoot." I am productive on the non-hardest problems and I was trying to mask, not on purpose mask, but who wants to be stuck on something so hard when there's so much else to do? From then on, I would show up to him with problems one and two and not talk about problems three through 100. Even if we were working on them, we would just not talk about them and we would get stuck on problems one and two. That was phenomenal advice, which I was like, "Oh, shoot, I'm going to be fired." But it was really a deeply impactful sentence.
turns.zh: 刚来这里工作的第一个月，我猜那是六七年前的事了，他们就让我负责我们的支付基础设施服务。这包括所有与金融系统对接的后端系统，以及我们构建外部API和产品所依托的内部API，涉及的内容相当广泛。我对金融一窍不通，对我们所谈论的业务规模也毫无概念。他们却疯狂地把这份责任交给了我。第一个月，我们举行季度业务回顾会……按照常规流程，我当时想：“好吧，很酷，下次我来写。”我刚来一个月。他们却说：“不，你来写。你的视角会更有价值。” 天哪，这简直让我崩溃。第四周，我被迫必须梳理整个业务流程，写这份文档来汇报我们的工作进展。这家公司在我来之前已经成立了七年，规模已经相当可观了。（02:31:54）：那真是高强度的工作，我记得写完初稿发给他时，他回复说：“这听起来不像你写的。”他逼我写这份文档的决心令人钦佩……这句话深深触动了我，我彻底重写了一遍，让它更符合我的风格，从那以后我也一直努力保持这种风格。（02:32:29）：约翰的批评更像是当头一棒。我向联合创始人约翰汇报工作，汇报九个月后，我会拿着写字板到处跑，疯狂地想完成所有任务。当时Stripe有很多事务要处理。我们每周一对一开会，我会列出所有已完成的任务、遇到的问题、需要升级协助的地方，以及卡住的难点……太多事情了。我用纸质清单，疯狂地翻来翻去。他说：“你是我们合作过的最善于解决三到一百个问题的员工之一，但我需要你专注于一和二。”（02:33:22）：天哪，这话真伤人。当时我：“哎呀，糟糕。”我确实更擅长处理不那么难的任务，却试图掩饰自己的无能。谁愿意在困难重重中纠缠不休？从那以后，我每次汇报只谈一和二的问题，哪怕我们正在处理其他任务，也绝不提及。真是个极具洞察力的建议，当时我觉得：“天啊，我要被炒鱿鱼了。” 但这句话确实影响深远。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, what a powerful, great, helpful... That's great advice [inaudible 02:34:10] right there.
turns.zh: 哇，多么有力、棒极了、太有帮助了……这真是绝佳的建议 [02:34:10的背景音]。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: He really looked my soul and-
turns.zh: 他真是看透了我的灵魂，

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love this.
turns.zh: 是啊，我太爱这个了。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Like a street fighter style or something.
turns.zh: 就像街头斗士的风格之类的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: But to your point, very impactful and helpful.
turns.zh: 但说到你提的，确实很有影响力，也很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是啊。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Jeff, we did it. The archeology is complete.
turns.zh: 杰夫，我们做到了！考古工作完成了。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: I appreciate the time, Lenny. It was fun. I don't do too many of these, so I'm curious to people's feedback and really appreciate the questions.
turns.zh: 莱尼，感谢你抽出时间。今天的交流很愉快。我不常参加这类活动，所以很期待大家的反馈，也非常感激你们提出的各种问题。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Jeff, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 太棒了。杰夫，非常感谢你能来。

turns.speaker: Jeff Weinstein
turns.en: Appreciate it, Lenny.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼。
